design_detail: NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation, HHE Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (November 2018): a 24-page report with a main report (pp. 1–6) and Supporting Technical Information (Sections A to D). A retrospective investigation, requested in May 2018 by a county sheriff's department (in Wisconsin, according to the keywords), of one incident in early 2018 in which two law enforcement officers became ill during a traffic-stop vehicle search after powder from a locked metal box blew into their faces. Methods: a site visit on 25–26 June 2018 with voluntary, confidential medical interviews of five officers who had been at the scene (including the two who became ill), discussions with command and risk-management staff, review of department policies, sheriff's department and state trooper incident reports, the EMS and emergency department records of the two officers, and the state forensic laboratory's results for the seized substances, discussed afterwards with a laboratory representative. NIOSH took no air, surface or skin samples, and neither NIOSH nor the treating clinicians tested blood or urine. Output: a narrative account, one table (Table C1, laboratory results), a discussion and three recommendations. Filed as a case report (one incident, two affected officers) and appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case reports and small case series without a comparison; although issued by a public body, it is a field investigation, not an evidence review or a statistics report, so the editors' evidence-report checklist is not used. No statistics.
can_establish: What happened in one incident in early 2018, as reconstructed from records and from interviews four months later: two officers reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion minutes after a powder blew into their faces; one was given naloxone by a colleague; the EMS and emergency department records show no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity (both alert and oriented, oxygen saturation normal, pupils normal-sized, heart and respiratory rates normal or raised, blood pressure raised); no biological test was done; and the state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC, but no fentanyl or other opioid, in the seized items, although a field test had been reported positive for fentanyl. It can also be cited for NIOSH's own statements and recommendations.
cannot_establish: Whether either officer absorbed any drug, which substance (if any) caused the symptoms, or whether stress, perceived risk or another condition contributed: no exposure measurement or biological testing was done, the composition of the powder that reached the officers is unknown, and perceived risk was not assessed. It says nothing about skin contact alone, since the powder reached the officers' faces and one officer's nose, and nothing about how often such incidents occur.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: the two officers who became ill in the single incident that the sheriff's department asked NIOSH to evaluate (request in May 2018; p. 1). Five officers who had been at the scene, including the two, gave voluntary, confidential medical interviews during the site visit of 25–26 June 2018 (p. B-1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable: the incident was chosen by the requesting employer.
sample.demographics: Not reported for either officer: age, sex, work history and medical history were discussed in the interviews but are not reported. The department had over 170 sworn officers and served a county of about 400,000 residents, with contract policing for seven municipalities of about 3,500 to 15,000 people, and had seen more incidents involving synthetic opioids in 2018 (p. A-1).
sample.selection_effects: A single incident, referred because officers became ill; incidents without symptoms, or not referred, are not represented, so nothing follows about how often such events happen or how often they involve drugs.

exposure.measurement: Not measured. The account comes from incident reports and interviews: a “plume of white powder” came from the seam of a locked metal box when one officer tilted it and blew into both officers' faces (p. B-2); the emergency physician recorded powder on both officers' faces and in one officer's nose (p. B-3). There was no air, surface or skin sampling and no blood or urine testing (the emergency department did no laboratory testing on either officer; p. B-3). The seized substances were field-tested by state agents, one reported presumptively positive for fentanyl (device, method and item not documented), and analysed by the state forensic laboratory (Table C1, p. C-1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: One brief contact with an unknown amount of powder of unknown composition. Routes NIOSH considers possible: inhalation, mucous membrane contact, ingestion, skin absorption, or a combination; earlier cross-contamination of gloves or equipment while handcuffing, patting down and seating the two vehicle occupants or searching the vehicle, followed by hand-to-face contact, is also considered possible (pp. 2, B-5 to B-6). When and how the officers were decontaminated is not known (p. B-5).
exposure.polysubstance: The box held items in which the laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC; alprazolam (in a 0.0013 g mixture) and sodium bicarbonate (in a 10.2071 g loose white powder) were only indicated, below the laboratory's reporting criteria for identification; no fentanyl or other opioid was identified (Table C1 with its footnotes, p. C-1; p. B-4). Which item, if any, formed the plume is not stated.

comparison.controls: None. NIOSH compares the officers' findings with textbook features of severe opioid toxicity (CNS depression, shallow or slow breathing, miosis, slow heart rate, low body temperature) and with the non-specific effects of stimulants and benzodiazepines (pp. B-4 to B-5). Other people at the scene are mentioned without symptoms (a third officer who lifted the box after the release and gave the naloxone; agents who handled the substances for field testing), but no comparison is drawn.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical histories were taken in the interviews but are not reported; NIOSH cannot completely rule out unrecognized medical conditions (p. B-6) and did not assess perceived risk (p. B-5).

outcomes.instruments: EMS and emergency department records: symptoms, blood pressure, heart and respiratory rates, oxygen saturation, oral temperature (emergency department), a three-lead ECG on one officer, blood glucose, pupil size, the EMS field assessment and the emergency physician's clinical impression; incident reports; interviews four months after the event; the state forensic laboratory's identification of the seized items (Table C1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical findings are set against textbook descriptions of opioid, stimulant and benzodiazepine toxicity (pp. B-4 to B-5); there is no exposure biomarker, and vital signs are given only as normal, elevated or decreased.
outcomes.operationalization: Health effects are the symptoms reported during the incident (difficulty breathing, dizziness, confusion) that stopped the officers working; exposure is contact with the powder as described; there is no criterion for drug exposure or for opioid toxicity beyond the clinical description.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The investigators knew the circumstances, and the emergency physician's clinical impression itself names a suspected opioid powder.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics: a narrative account of two cases. The only numerical results are the weights in Table C1 (p. C-1); the naloxone given at the scene was a 4 mg intranasal dose (p. B-2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; Health Hazard Evaluations are carried out on request under the Occupational Safety and Health Act (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Vital signs are reported only as categories, without values or times; the officer who received naloxone is not identified, and that officer's EMS findings are not given separately; the officers' medical histories, taken in interview, are not reported; the field test's device, method and the item that tested positive are not documented; the laboratory's methods and limits of detection, discussed with a laboratory representative, are not given; and Table C1 does not list some items the detective found in the box (a blue pill, glass pipes with burned residue, part of an apparent vape device), without saying whether they were tested.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Two officers had a powder of unknown composition blown into their faces and within minutes reported difficulty breathing, dizziness and confusion; one, described by colleagues as breathing shallowly and losing consciousness, was given 4 mg of intranasal naloxone by a colleague and was said to breathe better within minutes. When EMS arrived a few minutes later, both were alert and oriented, with raised blood pressure, heart and respiratory rates normal or raised and normal oxygen saturation; in the emergency department, temperature, heart and respiratory rates, oxygen saturation and pupil size were normal and blood pressure raised; no laboratory test was done; both were discharged after more than an hour without symptoms. The laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC in the seized items, only indicated alprazolam and sodium bicarbonate, and identified no fentanyl or other opioid, against a field test reported positive for fentanyl.
interpretation_gap.claimed: NIOSH's conclusions are hedged: no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity were seen, but the non-specific symptoms “could be consistent with milder toxicity related to drug exposure” (pp. 2, B-5, B-6 to B-7), and whether other clinical factors or perceived risk affected the health effects could not be determined (p. B-5). The framing goes further than the data in places: the title and the summary heading on health effects after “the exposure” presuppose an exposure to drugs that was never measured (p. 2); the text twice presents alprazolam as present (pp. 2, B-3) and discusses it as a CNS depressant the officers encountered (p. B-4), while Table C1 says it was only indicated (p. C-1); the colleagues' report of improvement after naloxone is not set against the EMS findings minutes later; and the report does not consider whether the plume could have been the loose white powder indicated as sodium bicarbonate, the only item described as a white powder in Table C1. The recommendations treat the incident as an exposure to be prevented; NIOSH also states that brief skin contact with powdered fentanyl is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (pp. 4, B-4, B-5).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, cited by NIOSH for the statement that brief skin contact is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (p. B-4; listed on p. D-2).
NIOSH interim guidance (a web topic page) on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, which this report applies (pp. 3–4; listed on p. D-2); not read.
This evaluation: incident in early 2018, request in May, site visit on 25–26 June, report in November.

Chiu et al., two NIOSH case investigations of officers' health effects after unintentional occupational opioid exposure (Am J Ind Med 62(5):439–447), as cited by Herman et al. (2020, ref 9); its first two authors share names with two of this report's authors, but whether this incident is one of the two cannot be told from either PDF; not read.
Herman et al.: none of 214 news articles on responder exposures (January 2012 to March 2018) described a confirmed exposure (card sc_herman_2020).

replication.where_it_stands: A single incident investigated after the event; replication does not apply. It adds one documented case to a picture in which reported poisonings of responders have not been confirmed by testing (Herman et al., 2020), and it applies NIOSH's interim guidance rather than testing it.

funding.funder: No funding statement. The evaluation was done by NIOSH staff under the Health Hazard Evaluation Program, which investigates workplace hazards under the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 and 42 CFR Part 85, at the request of the county sheriff's department (PDF p. 2; p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the report.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors David Jackson (MD), Sophia Chiu (MD, MPH) and Jennifer Hornsby-Myers (MS, CIH), with a named desktop publisher and medical field support (PDF p. 2). NIOSH, part of CDC, also issued the interim fentanyl guidance this report recommends (pp. 3–4). Copies went to the employer, employees and union, the state and local health departments and the OSHA regional office (PDF p. 2). External peer review is not described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Protocol-driven investigation of suspected responder exposures as they happen: blood sampled within hours and analysed by mass spectrometry for fentanyl, its analogues and the other drugs present; the material actually contacted collected and quantified, with air, surface and skin wipe samples; vital signs and pupil size recorded at first contact; and comparison with responders at the same scenes who had no symptoms. A series of such cases would show whether symptoms track measured drug exposure.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case reports and small case series without a comparison; most items do not apply to a single incident. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any conclusion about what caused the officers' illness, because exposure to a drug was never measured: no biological samples, no sampling of air, surfaces or skin, an undocumented field test contradicted by the laboratory, and no record of which item formed the plume. The report may be cited, attributed to NIOSH, for: the incident as reconstructed; the absence of any laboratory testing of either officer; the clinical findings recorded by EMS and the emergency department, which showed no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity; the forensic laboratory's identification of cocaine, methamphetamine and THC and of no fentanyl or other opioid, despite a presumptive field result for fentanyl; NIOSH's statements that brief skin contact with powdered fentanyl is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed and that field tests vary widely; and its recommendations, as its own. It may not be cited as a case of fentanyl or opioid poisoning, as evidence of absorption through the skin, as evidence that the symptoms were psychological (not assessed), or for how often such incidents occur.

key_findings.finding: In May 2018 a county sheriff's department asked NIOSH to evaluate unintentional exposure of its officers to illicit drugs, after an incident during a traffic stop in early 2018 in which two officers developed adverse health effects. NIOSH visited on 25–26 June 2018, met officers involved and command staff, reviewed policies and reviewed sheriff's department and state trooper incident reports, state forensic laboratory results for the substances submitted, and the two officers' medical records.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Request, 1st paragraph; Our Approach, lead sentence and bulleted lists (PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: During the site visit NIOSH held voluntary, confidential medical interviews with five officers who had been at the scene, including the two who became ill, covering the incident, work history and practices, protective equipment, medical history and health effects; it reviewed the EMS and emergency department records of the two, spoke with the detective who packaged the seized substances, and discussed the laboratory's methods and results with a laboratory representative. Apart from the presumptive result, no information on the field test was available.
key_findings.locator: Section B › Methods: Description of the Incident, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. B-1, PDF p. 13); Methods: Medical Record Review and Methods: Forensic Analyses of Substances Found at the Response (p. B-3, PDF p. 15)
key_findings.note: No section of the report describes air, surface, skin, blood or urine sampling, and p. B-3 states that no laboratory testing was done on either officer (editors' reading of the whole report).

key_findings.finding: A vehicle that had left its lane three times was stopped; after a K-9 unit indicated drugs, the two officers handcuffed, patted down and seated the two occupants in separate squad cars, then searched the vehicle by hand, finding sandwich bags, an open box of baking soda, steel wool, cut straws, a glass pipe with apparent marijuana residue, apparent marijuana and a locked metal box under the passenger seat. They did not report seeing any unknown powder before or during the search; a short time later one officer tilted the box, and a plume of white powder came from the seam of the lid and blew into both officers' faces; a third officer then lifted the box, and no powder was seen beneath it.
key_findings.locator: Section B › Results: Description of the Incident, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 13–14)

key_findings.finding: At the time there was no written policy on protective equipment for unknown powders; both officers wore long-sleeved uniforms, one leather gloves and the other latex and Kevlar gloves; nitrile gloves were not available; neither wore a respirator, although all of the department's officers had been quantitatively fit-tested for N95 filtering facepiece respirators.
key_findings.locator: Results: Description of the Incident, 2nd paragraph (p. B-2, PDF p. 14); Discussion › Issues related to exposure, 1st paragraph (p. B-5, PDF p. 17)

key_findings.finding: A few minutes after the release both officers reported difficulty breathing, confusion and dizziness. When one appeared to develop shallow breathing and to be quickly losing consciousness, the third officer gave that officer a 4 mg intranasal dose of naloxone; breathing was noted to improve within minutes, and EMS arrived a few minutes later and took both officers to an emergency department. The summary attributes the positive response to naloxone to other officers' reports and does not say which officer was treated.
key_findings.locator: Results: Description of the Incident, 4th paragraph (p. B-2, PDF p. 14); Our Key Findings › LEOs 1 and 2 experienced work-related health effects after the exposure, 1st and 3rd bullets (p. 2, PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: EMS found both officers alert and oriented; one reported feeling dizzy and the other short of breath. Vital signs en route showed raised blood pressure, heart and respiratory rates normal to raised and normal oxygen saturation without supplemental oxygen; a three-lead ECG on one officer showed no abnormality; blood glucose was mildly low to normal. The EMS field assessment was environment, poisoning or drug ingestion.
key_findings.locator: Section B › Results: Medical Record Review, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: In the emergency department the physician noted in the record that the powder had got on both officers' faces during the incident and into one officer's nose; oral temperatures were normal, blood pressures raised, heart and respiratory rates normal, oxygen saturation normal on room air and pupils normal-sized. No laboratory testing was done on either officer. Both stayed without symptoms throughout an observation period of over an hour and were discharged home; the clinical impression for both was work-related suspected exposure to an opioid or derivative powder.
key_findings.locator: Results: Medical Record Review, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: A sheriff's department detective, wearing a full-body Tyvek suit with rubber gloves and a self-contained breathing apparatus, processed the vehicle; agents forced the box open (contents as quoted in the report from an unnamed record: glass pipes with burned residue, a small bag of marijuana, part of an apparent vape device, a blue pill, a bag of a large white powdery substance, a small bag thought to hold methamphetamine and a smaller bag of white rock), took the substances to a remote location for field testing and advised the detective that one of them was positive for fentanyl. The state forensic laboratory identified cocaine, methamphetamine and THC, and did not identify fentanyl or any other opioid in the evidence samples sent for testing.
key_findings.locator: Results: Description of the Incident, 5th paragraph (p. B-2, PDF p. 14); Methods and Results: Forensic Analyses of Substances Found at the Response (pp. B-3 to B-4, PDF pp. 15–16)

key_findings.finding: Table C1 lists nine items, all from the locked box: a loose white powdery substance, 10.2071 g, sodium bicarbonate indicated; an off-white chunky substance, 5.2883 g, cocaine; crystalline material, 2.6043 g, methamphetamine; plant material, 0.6531 g, tetrahydrocannabinol; loose crystalline material, 0.0545 g, and crystalline material, 0.0483 g, both methamphetamine; a gray powdery substance, 0.0117 g, cocaine and methamphetamine; tiny yellow chunks with crystalline material, 0.0013 g, methamphetamine, cocaine and alprazolam (indicated); and residue with no weight, cocaine and methamphetamine. Indicated means that the examinations did not meet the laboratory's reporting criteria for identification. Weights exclude residues; no purity, concentrations, methods or limits of detection are given.
key_findings.locator: Section C, Table C1 and its footnotes (PDF p. 20)

key_findings.finding: NIOSH lists the classic signs of severe opioid toxicity (lethargy or other CNS depression, shallow or slow breathing, miosis, slow heart rate, low body temperature), noting that not every patient shows all of them and that low-dose exposure may cause milder symptoms; that stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine can cause similar non-specific symptoms (classically raised heart rate and blood pressure; also shortness of breath, dizziness, confusion and headache), and alprazolam drowsiness and dizziness; that effects of combinations below life-threatening levels may be hard to tell apart and adulterants may contribute; and that it could not determine whether other clinical factors or perceived risk, which is associated with anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure, affected the officers' health effects, as this was not assessed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues related to health effects, 2nd to 5th paragraphs (PDF pp. 16–17)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the two officers developed health effects shortly after exposure to a powder suspected to be illicit drugs; the field test was presumptively positive for fentanyl, but the laboratory did not detect fentanyl or any other opioid; the providers who evaluated both officers saw no objective signs of serious opioid toxicity; NIOSH considers it possible that the non-specific symptoms might fit milder toxicity from drug exposure, without asserting it; and the symptoms were severe enough that the officers needed medical attention and could not continue their duties.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph (PDF pp. 18–19); also Our Key Findings, p. 2, last bullet of the health-effects list

key_findings.finding: NIOSH states, citing the Interagency Board (2017), the ACMT–AACT position statement (Moss et al., 2017) and its own 2017 guidance, that brief skin contact with powdered fentanyl or its analogues is not expected to lead to toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed, and names inhalation, mucous membrane contact, ingestion and percutaneous exposure (for example, needlestick) as the routes of greatest concern. In this incident, when or how the officers were decontaminated is not known.
key_findings.locator: Recommendation 1, Why? box, 1st paragraph (p. 4, PDF p. 8); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. B-4, PDF p. 16); Discussion › Issues related to exposure, 2nd paragraph (p. B-5, PDF p. 17)

key_findings.finding: NIOSH notes that, as with other similar incidents among emergency responders, this incident was evaluated retrospectively four months later, happened quickly in a setting where advance planning is difficult, and involved highly toxic materials not fully characterized from an occupational safety and health perspective (NIOSH's wording); that because the powder blew into the officers' faces, inhalation, mucous membrane absorption, ingestion, skin absorption or a combination are all possible; and that gloves or equipment may have been cross-contaminated while handcuffing, patting down and seating the vehicle occupants or searching the vehicle, with later hand-to-face contact.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues related to exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF pp. 17–18)

key_findings.finding: NIOSH attributes the discrepancy between the field and laboratory results possibly to differences in sensitivity and specificity, notes that both analyses were done primarily for law enforcement, not to characterize occupational health risks, and states that field-testing methods vary widely (some detect traces of known drugs in the nanogram to microgram range, others only bulk drugs in microgram to milligram amounts, and an instrument identifies only drugs in its library), that failure to identify a substance does not completely rule out a hazardous drug, and that, without well-validated field tests, officers should treat unknown powders as possibly containing fentanyl regardless of field results.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues related to exposure, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (PDF p. 18); the same points in summary on pp. 2–3

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: a retrospective investigation; interviews four months after the incident; exposures not fully characterized; and unrecognized medical conditions cannot be completely ruled out despite the review of the EMS and emergency department records.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 18)

key_findings.finding: After its own review the department was developing a policy on protective equipment for handling opioids and unknown substances, updating its bloodborne-pathogen and naloxone policies, improving intranasal naloxone access and training, and improving access to nitrile gloves, disposable sleeves, P100 filtering facepiece respirators and eye protection.
key_findings.locator: Our Key Findings › The sheriff's department identified areas for improvement after the incident, paragraph and bullets (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: NIOSH's recommendations, its own and framed for this department: (1) continue revising the work practices the department identified, following NIOSH's fentanyl guidance for emergency responders, in particular not touching the eyes, mouth or nose after touching possibly contaminated surfaces; no field testing of unknown powders suspected to be fentanyl, because of the added exposure risk, except by specifically trained personnel in protective equipment when identification is critical; treating unknown powders as possibly containing fentanyl regardless of field results; avoiding tasks that make drugs airborne; washing exposed skin with soap and water (or water), not hand sanitizer or bleach; nitrile gloves when drugs are suspected (exposure counted as minimal under NIOSH guidance when drugs are suspected but not visible), with training in removing and changing gloves; more protective equipment depending on the scene; attention to state and Interagency Board guidance; a job safety analysis covering respirator use, communication while wearing protective equipment and glove procedures; and training; (2) joint training and uniform procedures with neighbouring police, fire and EMS agencies; (3) encouraging officers to report possible exposures and health effects to supervisors, for review together with forensic results.
key_findings.locator: Our Recommendations; Recommendations 1 to 3 with their Why? boxes and action lists (PDF pp. 7–10)

B-3), and the Discussion counts it among the CNS depressants the officers encountered (p. B-4), but the footnote to Table C1 says alprazolam was only indicated, the examinations not meeting the reporting criteria for identification, in a 0.0013 g mixture (p. C-1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Alprazolam's presence is not established; its place among the possible explanations for the officers' symptoms rests on an indication.

B-3) but may overstate the observation; the summary has symptoms resolving during monitoring, whereas the record review has both officers asymptomatic throughout observation and the Discussion has symptoms mostly resolved by arrival; the technical section, based on the records, is the one to cite.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary overstates the length of observation and places the resolution of symptoms later than the records do; the technical section, based on the records, is the one to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The report never says which item formed the plume or which item gave the presumptive field result, yet it speaks of the powder in the box as if one identified material had been tested (pp. B-4, B-6). The only item described as a white powder in Table C1 is the loose 10.2071 g item indicated as sodium bicarbonate, and the officers had seen an open box of baking soda in the vehicle (p. B-2); the report does not discuss whether the plume could have been that material.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the officers were exposed to any drug at all cannot be established from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: Items in the report's quoted list of the box's contents (its source not named: a blue pill, glass pipes with burned residue, part of an apparent vape device) do not appear in Table C1, and the report does not say whether they were tested. Page: pp. B-2, C-1. Consequence unchanged.
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding of no opioid applies to the items listed in Table C1.

reporting_issues.issue: Although NIOSH discussed the analytic methods with a laboratory representative, the report gives no methods or limits of detection for the laboratory analysis, while noting, for field tests, that failure to identify a substance does not completely rule out a hazardous drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: The laboratory's negative result for fentanyl cannot be read against a detection limit; nothing reported excludes trace amounts.

reporting_issues.issue: Vital signs are given only as categories, without values or times; the officer who received naloxone is not identified and that officer's EMS findings are not given separately; the improvement after naloxone is reported from colleagues' observations.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reported response to naloxone cannot be checked against measurements; minutes later EMS recorded both officers alert and oriented, with respiratory rates normal or raised and normal oxygen saturation.

design_detail: Qualitative interview study (Research paper, Int J Drug Policy 95, article 103303), the qualitative component of a larger mixed-methods study of law enforcement agency naloxone programmes in the United States, run by RTI International with the Police Executive Research Forum as study partner and supported by Arnold Ventures. Semi-structured interviews, January to May 2020, with 38 people at five purposively chosen law enforcement agencies; this paper reports only the 23 officers and agency leaders, of whom 20 were asked four open-ended questions on fentanyl (whether officers are at risk of overdose if they come in contact with fentanyl; whether officers are concerned about this on scene; training, policies or procedures for handling suspected fentanyl; where they first heard about exposure). Interviews were recorded and transcribed; the team debriefed after each site visit, built a master list of codes, coded in NVivo 12 and had coded data verified by a second team member. Findings are presented as themes with unattributed quotations and verbal quantifiers (nearly all, a few, over one third, a handful), without counts per theme. The dispatch brief describes this paper as a survey of officers; the paper itself is an interview study, and the national agency survey it says the interviews will inform (expected to field in early 2021, p. 2) is not reported here.
can_establish: What these 23 officers and leaders in five US agencies said in 2020 about their risk from encountering fentanyl, where they had heard about officer exposures, what training and precautions their agencies had, and that officers who had heard of a colleague's overdose could not confirm either the substance or the overdose.
cannot_establish: How common the belief is among US police (a purposive sample chosen through agency contacts, reported with quantifiers but no counts), whether any officer was actually exposed to or poisoned by fentanyl, or what the risk of touching fentanyl is, which the paper takes from the ACMT/AACT position statement and other guidance rather than from its own data.

sample.recruitment: Agencies first, then people. Five agencies were chosen to represent different community characteristics (population size, geography, overdose mortality), agency characteristics (number of sworn officers, budget) and overdose-response characteristics (presence and maturity of a naloxone programme, partnerships); Site 5 was chosen because its leadership had decided not to equip officers with naloxone (Methods › Recruitment, 1st paragraph, p. 2). The team, including the Police Executive Research Forum, invited each police chief by email, with a telephone follow-up 3–4 business days later; one agency declined and one could not schedule, and each was replaced by the agency of a neighbouring community (editors' count: seven agencies approached, five took part). At each site an agency lead, usually the captain or manager overseeing the naloxone programme (the chief at the site without one), identified 4–11 officers, leaders and community partners to interview (Recruitment, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). There were no participant refusals (Data collection, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Officers who had administered naloxone at least once to someone they believed to be overdosing, officers who had responded to an overdose without administering naloxone, and leaders who supervised naloxone programmes; all aged 18 or over (Participants, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Community partners and EMS or fire representatives were interviewed but excluded from this analysis (Participants, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).
sample.demographics: Of the 23 officers and leaders, 15 were Caucasian and 18 male; law enforcement experience ranged from 18 to 33 years among leaders and from 2 to 22 years among officers (Participants, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). Sites (Table 1, p. 3): West, jurisdiction over 1,000,000, naloxone programme since 2017; Midwest, 250,000–999,999, since 2016; South and Northeast, each 25,000–249,000, since 2015; South, under 25,000, no naloxone programme. Age, rank distribution and the agency of each respondent are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). Three of the 23 officers and leaders were not asked the fentanyl questions; the reason is not given (Qualitative study instrument, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Interviewees were picked by agency contacts who ran the naloxone programmes, and 12 of the 17 officers had administered naloxone, so the sample leans towards officers engaged in overdose response. Agencies were chosen purposively and two were substitutes. The authors state that respondents were not selected randomly and that the responses do not reflect law enforcement generally or even the agencies the respondents work for (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 5). Interviews were arranged through agency leadership.

exposure.measurement: No exposure was measured: the study concerns beliefs and reported experiences. The exposures mentioned (two officers' own past contact with fentanyl without opioid overdose symptoms; colleagues' overdoses that officers had heard about) are interviewees' reports, not verified by the study; asked for confirmation, no officer could say with certainty that the substance was fentanyl or that the colleague had overdosed (Results › Source of information regarding fentanyl, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 4).

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Leaders and officers are described together; differences between agencies, ranks or naloxone experience are not analysed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Prior training content, media exposure, anxiety and personal experiences that might shape beliefs were explored only through the open questions.

outcomes.instruments: Semi-structured interview guide developed by the study team for the larger naloxone-programme study, with four open-ended fentanyl questions and follow-up probes (Qualitative study instrument, 2nd paragraph, p. 3): whether officers are “at risk of overdose if they come in contact with fentanyl”; whether officers are concerned that contact on scene might put them at risk of overdose; training, policies or procedures for safe handling of suspected fentanyl; and where they first heard about exposure to fentanyl. 34 interviews were done in person by three-person teams (lead interviewer, co-lead, notetaker) and the last four, at Site 4, by Zoom; all were recorded and transcribed (Data collection, pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. No saturation criterion, member checking, reflexivity statement or reporting checklist (such as COREQ) is mentioned.
outcomes.operationalization: Belief was neither defined nor rated: themes were coded under the codes fentanyl exposure and fentanyl handling risks (Analysis, p. 3). The questions asked about risk of overdose from contact with fentanyl in general, without separating touch from inhalation or risk from lethality; a handful of respondents were also asked whether they knew the ACMT/AACT statement (p. 4).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Coded data were verified by at least one other site team member before being finalized (Analysis, p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: None, and none would be appropriate for this design. Findings are reported with verbal quantifiers and almost no counts: nearly all officers who were asked said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of overdose, while a few did not see it as more dangerous than other duties (p. 3); only a handful had received specialized training on handling suspected fentanyl (pp. 3–4); most officers always put on gloves for a suspected overdose call (p. 4); over one third of officers had heard of someone in their own agency overdosing, from three agencies (p. 4); two officers reported their own exposure without symptoms (p. 4); a handful were asked about the ACMT/AACT statement (p. 4). The denominator of each quantifier (17 officers, 20 asked, or 23 officers and leaders) is not stated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The overall study, including the qualitative component, was reviewed and approved by RTI International's Institutional Review Board (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2); informed consent was obtained before the interviews (p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the officers' and leaders' interviews are analysed (23 of 38). Quotations carry no respondent identifier, rank or site, so it cannot be seen whether a theme rests on few people. A community partner, a group the Methods exclude from this analysis, is quoted in the Results (pp. 2, 4).
analysis.power: Not applicable. No sampling target or saturation criterion is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among the 20 officers and leaders asked, nearly all said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of overdose, while a few saw it as no more dangerous than their other duties (no counts). Officers had heard about exposures from other officers, law enforcement professional organizations, a DEA roll-call video shown at in-service training and regional intelligence bulletins. Over one third of officers had heard of someone in their own agency overdosing, but none could say with certainty that the substance was fentanyl or that the colleague had overdosed. Two officers described their own exposure without opioid overdose symptoms. Only one of the five sites had a fentanyl-handling module, and a handful asked about the ACMT/AACT statement did not know it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that “Nearly all leaders and officers interviewed wrongly believed that dermal exposure to fentanyl was deadly” (p. 1). The Results describe concern about risk of overdose from encountering fentanyl among those asked (20 of 23), with exceptions, and the questions asked about contact in general, not about skin contact being deadly (p. 3). The Discussion says nearly all officers interviewed believe fentanyl is a significant occupational hazard with possibly fatal outcomes (p. 4), and that the extreme measures at one agency instilled even greater fear in its officers (p. 5), which rests on one officer's account of his agency's policy change (p. 4). The statements that the risk to responders is extremely low and that symptoms in media accounts match panic rather than opioid toxicity come from the ACMT/AACT statement and other guidance cited in the Introduction (pp. 1–2), not from this study. The limitations paragraph says plainly that the sample was small, not random and not generalizable (p. 5).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT joint position statement on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, cited (as ACMT, 2017) for the extremely low risk of clinically significant exposure (p. 2); the record moss_2017 has the same title.
Persaud and Jennings (2019): survey of New York first responders, cited as finding that nearly 80% believed even briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (p. 2); not read.
Beletsky et al. (2020): analysis of news coverage and Facebook sharing, cited for uncorrected media stories and their sharing (pp. 2, 5) (card sc_beletsky_2020).
Herman et al. (2020): media reports of responder exposures, cited for misinformation in the media (p. 5); not read for this card.

Winograd et al. (2020): before training, only 20.9% of 140 Missouri emergency responders answered False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl; cited in the Discussion for a brief presentation reducing the belief (p. 5) (card sc_winograd_2020).
This study published; the national law enforcement agency survey it was to inform is not reported in it.

del Pozo et al. (2021): before training, 103 of 129 Indiana officers (79.8%) agreed that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it; cites this study (card sc_del_pozo_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: The finding that most US first responders asked believe contact with fentanyl puts them at risk of overdose recurs in surveys by other teams, with different items and samples: the baselines of two training evaluations (Winograd et al., 2020, Missouri, about 79% not answering False; del Pozo et al., 2021, Indiana, 79.8% agreeing) and a New York survey cited here (Persaud and Jennings, 2019; not read). None is a probability sample of police. Where the belief comes from (peers, professional bodies, a DEA video, intelligence bulletins) has been described only qualitatively, in this study.

funding.funder: The overall study was supported by Arnold Ventures under Grant 19-02661; the same section states that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of this article, and that the content does not represent the official views of Arnold Ventures (Funding sources, p. 5). The Acknowledgements thank the Arnold Ventures grant manager for guidance on the study design and the Police Executive Research Forum partners for guidance on the overall study (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (Declarations of Interest, p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: RTI International (Division for Applied Justice Research; Community Health Research Division) and the University of California, San Diego (Department of Medicine, Division of Global Public Health) (p. 1). The Police Executive Research Forum was a study partner and part of the team that contacted the police chiefs (p. 2). The funding statement is internally inconsistent (grant support, yet no financial support for the research). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For how common the belief is: a probability-sample survey of US police officers with a reported response rate and items that separate touching from inhaling and any risk from risk of death, repeated over time. For officers' accounts of colleagues' poisonings: prospective review of reported exposures with toxicological testing of the officer and of the substance.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: Interviews suit the aim of exploring knowledge and fear, but the stated purpose is to detail the extent of the belief (p. 2), a question of frequency that a purposive interview sample cannot answer; the fentanyl questions were a small part of an interview about naloxone programmes.

domains.domain: Sampling strategy
domains.note: Purposive choice of agencies (two of them substitutes) and of interviewees by agency leads who ran the naloxone programmes; 12 of the 17 officers had administered naloxone; no saturation criterion; 3 of the 23 were not asked the key questions.

domains.domain: Data collection
domains.note: Semi-structured interviews by three-person teams, recorded and transcribed, four of them by Zoom; but the fentanyl questions were not put to everyone, the ACMT/AACT question only to a handful, leaders were asked about their officers' concerns (second-hand), and interviews were arranged through agency leadership.

domains.domain: Relationship between researchers and participants (reflexivity)
domains.note: No reflexive account. The Introduction frames the belief as erroneous before the data are presented (pp. 1–2), and the funder's grant manager advised on study design (p. 5); how this shaped questioning and coding is not discussed.

domains.domain: Ethics
domains.note: Institutional review board approval (RTI International), informed consent before interviews, recording with consent, no identifying information retained, agencies anonymized (pp. 2–3).

domains.domain: Rigour of analysis
domains.note: The analytic approach is not named; codes were built from debriefing notes and interview notes were compiled in a spreadsheet, while the qualitative data were coded in NVivo; coded data were checked by a second team member, but no double coding, negative-case analysis or audit trail is described (p. 3).

domains.domain: Clarity and grounding of findings
domains.note: Themes are illustrated by quotations, but without identifiers; quantifiers lack denominators; the abstract's wording (dermal exposure believed deadly) is sharper than the question asked and the theme reported; a community partner, outside the analysed group, is quoted.

domains.domain: Transferability as claimed
domains.note: The limitations state that the responses do not reflect law enforcement generally or even the agencies studied (p. 5).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a qualitative study with the editors' checklist. The interviews are a credible account of what these officers and leaders said and of the routes by which the belief reached them. The limits are a purposive, agency-selected sample, unexplained gaps in who was asked what, quantifiers without counts, and an abstract that sharpens the finding. Citable for: concern about overdose from encountering fentanyl voiced by nearly all of those asked in five agencies in 2020; the sources officers named (peers, professional organizations, a DEA training video, intelligence bulletins); officers' second-hand accounts of colleagues' overdoses being unconfirmed; one agency's protective measures. Not citable for: the prevalence of the belief among US police, or anything about the toxicological risk of touching fentanyl.

key_findings.finding: 38 people were interviewed at five agencies between January and May 2020 (34 in person, January to March; the last four, at Site 4, by Zoom in April and May). The paper analyses the 23 officers and leaders: 12 officers who had administered naloxone, 5 officers who had responded to overdoses without administering it, and 6 leaders; 15 were Caucasian and 18 male; experience 18–33 years among leaders and 2–22 years among officers.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Data collection, 1st paragraph (starts p. 2, continues p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The five agencies were chosen purposively for diversity, Site 5 because its leadership had decided not to equip officers with naloxone; one agency declined and one could not schedule, and both were replaced by neighbouring communities; agency leads identified 4–11 interviewees per site; there were no participant refusals.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Recruitment, 1st–2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Data collection, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: 20 of the 23 officers and leaders were asked the fentanyl questions: whether officers are at risk of overdose if they come in contact with fentanyl; whether officers are concerned that contact on scene might put them at risk of overdose; what training, policies or procedures exist for handling suspected fentanyl; and where they first heard about exposure.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Qualitative study instrument, 2nd paragraph and its bulleted questions

key_findings.finding: Nearly all officers who were asked said they were concerned that encountering fentanyl might put them at risk of overdose; a few, including a leader who is quoted, did not see it as more dangerous than their other duties. No counts are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Officers perceptions of fentanyl exposure, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (block quotations not counted)

key_findings.finding: Only a handful had ever received specialized training or updated policies on handling substances suspected to be fentanyl; one respondent said their academy was adding fentanyl-handling procedures to in-service training. Of the five sites, representatives from only one mentioned having incorporated a module on handling fentanyl, and the Discussion describes the one agency that provided guidance as using extreme measures, including personal protective equipment, calling hazmat teams and ending field testing of suspected drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Training for handling fentanyl, 1st paragraph (starts p. 3, continues p. 4); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: One agency required a gas mask and gloves for field testing any white powder or pill; an officer reported that his agency had stopped field testing drugs because of exposure concerns; most officers said they always put on gloves when going to a suspected overdose, although this was not a formal procedure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes to agency policy and officer behavior, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Asked how they had heard of officers being exposed to fentanyl and overdosing, several officers named other officers or law enforcement professional organizations; one had learned from a DEA video shown at annual in-service training that fentanyl could be absorbed through the skin or inhaled; a leader referred to regional intelligence-centre information about officers overdosing from touching it or from it being in the air, and an officer recalled a bulletin story about an officer touching fentanyl that gave no details of what happened.
key_findings.locator: Results › Source of information regarding fentanyl, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Over one third of officers reported having heard of someone in their own agency overdosing (officers from three agencies). Asked for confirmation, no officer could say with certainty that the substance was fentanyl or that the officer had overdosed, nor in most cases whether the officer was taken to hospital. Two officers said they had been exposed to fentanyl themselves and had no symptoms of opioid overdose, but remained very concerned.
key_findings.locator: Results › Source of information regarding fentanyl, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (the 3rd continues into the right column)
key_findings.note: The denominator of over one third is not stated (17 officers, 20 asked, or 23 officers and leaders).

key_findings.finding: A handful of respondents asked whether they knew the ACMT/AACT joint statement on dermal exposure did not know it and were surprised by its conclusion that dermal and inhalation exposure pose low risk to first responders.
key_findings.locator: Results › Source of information regarding fentanyl, 7th (last) paragraph

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that nearly all leaders and officers interviewed wrongly believed dermal exposure to fentanyl was deadly; the Discussion, that nearly all officers interviewed believe fentanyl is a significant occupational hazard with possibly fatal outcomes, despite no confirmed case of an officer overdosing after encountering fentanyl on the job.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 1); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The authors' summary; see the interpretation gap for how it differs from the question asked and the theme reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says nearly all leaders and officers interviewed believed dermal exposure was deadly, but only 20 of the 23 were asked, the questions concerned risk of overdose from contact in general, the Results describe concern about risk with a few exceptions, and no counts are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's wording cannot be cited as a measured prevalence of a specific belief; cite the Results as concern voiced by nearly all of those asked.

reporting_issues.issue: Quantifiers are given without denominators (nearly all, a few, most, a handful, over one third of officers).
reporting_issues.consequence: No share can be calculated; over one third could mean as few as 6 of the 17 officers (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods restrict the analysis to officers and leaders (n = 23) and exclude community partners, but the Results quote a community partner with more than 20 years of experience working with law enforcement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the quoted view concerns leadership buy-in, not fentanyl risk, but it shows the analysed group was not kept strictly apart.

reporting_issues.issue: The Funding section states both that the overall study was supported by an Arnold Ventures grant (19-02661) and that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of this article.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether this paper's work was grant-funded; the Acknowledgements also credit the grant manager with guidance on the study design.

reporting_issues.issue: The Analysis describes interview notes compiled in a spreadsheet and a master list of codes built from site debriefing notes, and then says the qualitative data were coded in NVivo 12, without saying whether the transcripts (which Data collection says were made) or the notes were coded.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for a thematic description; it limits judgment of how closely the themes follow what was said.

design_detail: Short Report (Int J Drug Policy 86, article 102951): a retrospective content analysis of online news. Between May and December 2019 the authors searched the open-source Media Cloud news database for articles published January 2015 to September 2019, using the query fentanyl AND (glove* OR mask* OR touch* OR contact* OR absor* OR inhal* OR breath* OR expos*); screened the results for relevance and duplicates; and coded each article as misinformation, corrective or partially corrective. Four trained reviewers (staff and student interns) coded redundantly, and a staff member resolved discordant codes. Facebook shares per article came from Media Cloud via CrowdTangle; potential reach was modelled as shares multiplied by 155, an average number of contacts per person (Dunbar, 2016), giving an upper bound on views rather than unique viewers. The units are news articles, not people, and the only social media measure is Facebook shares of those articles. Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist adapted to articles, as for sc_barnett_2021. The PDF opens with Elsevier's COVID-19 resource-centre permission notice (PDF p. 1, not part of the article); the article is printed pp. 1–3 (p. 1 unnumbered) on PDF pp. 2–4, and anchors cite the printed pages. The online Supplement (Figs 2–3, cited in the text for the DEA statement and the East Liverpool story) is not among the files.
can_establish: How many online news articles retrieved by this Media Cloud search (January 2015 to September 2019) the authors coded as presenting overdose risk from casual contact with fentanyl as real, or as reporting such incidents, against articles correcting it, and how many Facebook shares each group received.
cannot_establish: How many people saw, read or believed these articles (reach is an upper bound from an assumed multiplier), whether the coverage or government statements caused officers' fears, laws or delays in overdose response, or whether casual contact with fentanyl is dangerous, which the paper takes from the ACMT/AACT statement while the outcomes of the incidents it describes come from news reports.

sample.recruitment: Not people: online news articles in Media Cloud, an open-source web-scraping media analysis tool whose content collections, built by geography or topic, the authors queried for content related to the overdose crisis (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Articles published January 2015 to September 2019 that matched the nine-term query, reviewed for relevance and duplication (Methods, 1st–2nd paragraphs, p. 2). The relevance criteria, language, the collections used and the number of hits before screening are not reported.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Articles spanned 48 states, most of them from Texas and Pennsylvania; counts by state are not given (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; the number of articles excluded at screening is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Coverage depends on Media Cloud, which the authors say is sometimes limited by paywalls and by differences in archiving, and whose capabilities set the 2015 start (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 3). Television, radio, police bulletins and social media posts themselves are outside the frame; social media enters only as Facebook shares of the retrieved articles.

exposure.measurement: Not a drug exposure. Each article's title, text and media captions were coded under a standardized protocol into one of three categories; Facebook shares were taken from Media Cloud via CrowdTangle (Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 2).

comparison.controls: Corrective and partially corrective articles are the comparison for misinformation articles (article counts, shares and modelled reach). There is no comparison with coverage of other drugs or with police assessments of occupational risk, as the authors note (p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Article features that could explain sharing (outlet size, video, date, incident) were not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Three-category coding of each article; Facebook share counts; modelled potential reach (shares × 155) (Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 2). Coders also noted the state of publication, the incidents covered and any reference to government guidance.
outcomes.validity_norms: No codebook is published and no inter-rater agreement statistic is reported; discordant codes were resolved by a staff member (SS). The multiplier of 155 is taken from the literature, not measured for these articles.
outcomes.operationalization: Misinformation: content that explicitly endorsed overdose risk from casual contact (by touch or inhalation) or transmission, or that presented anecdotal accounts of such events mentioning the rumoured sequelae (overdose, shortness of breath, heart palpitations, fainting), with ACMT 2017 as the reference. Corrective: content that accurately communicated the lack of immediate health risk or explicitly debunked the narrative. Partially corrective: both, through incomplete description of risks or mixed reviews of anecdotes. There is no neutral category, so an article that reported an officer's account without endorsing it counts as misinformation (Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 2).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; coders were project staff and student interns applying the authors' definitions.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and share totals only, without any measure of uncertainty. 506 of 551 articles were coded misinformation (printed 92%; 91.8% by editors' calculation), with 450,011 Facebook shares; 45 were corrective or partially corrective (8%), with 48,235 shares; 18 were unequivocally corrective, with 29,652 shares (Results, p. 2). Editors' calculations: the abstract's factor of 15 equals 450,011/29,652 = 15.2, misinformation against the 18 unequivocally corrective articles only; against all 45 corrective or partially corrective articles the ratio is 450,011/48,235 = 9.3, the Results' roughly one-tenth. The printed 6.6% of total for the 18 articles equals 29,652/450,011; their share of all 498,246 shares is 6.0%. Modelled reach is shares × 155: 450,011 × 155 = 69,751,705 and 29,652 × 155 = 4,596,060 potential views, as printed.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. No human subjects were involved (Ethics, p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Counts by state, outlet and incident (other than two incidents and the 80 articles referring to the DEA video), the number of hits before screening and inter-rater agreement are not reported. Fig. 1 shows monthly series without printed values. The Supplement figures were not available for this reading.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 551 relevant articles (47 national, 504 state and local), 506 were coded misinformation, under a definition that includes reports of anecdotal incidents, and 45 corrective or partially corrective, 18 of them unequivocally corrective. Misinformation articles had 450,011 Facebook shares, against 48,235 for corrective or partially corrective articles and 29,652 for the unequivocally corrective ones. The first notable surge of coverage coincided with a 2016 DEA statement, whose video appeared in 80 articles. The two most-shared incidents, as described from news reports, were an East Liverpool, Ohio officer whose powder and overdose were never confirmed by laboratory testing, and a Columbus, Ohio officer whose substance was later confirmed as methamphetamine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says misinformation was “potentially reaching nearly 70,000,000 users” and the Discussion speaks of the potential exposure of 70 million people on Facebook (pp. 1, 3), while the Results call the same figure an upper bound on potential views “(as opposed to unique viewers)” (p. 2), obtained by multiplying shares by an assumed 155 contacts. The abstract's factor of 15 uses the narrowest corrective group (18 articles); with all corrective or partially corrective content the ratio is about 9 (editors' calculation). “Amplified by erroneous government statements” (abstract, p. 1) rests on a surge coinciding with the 2016 DEA statement and on 80 articles referring to its video; amplification was not analysed. The Background's statements that fentanyl panic complicated overdose rescue, rationalized punitive laws and wasted money, and the Discussion's statement that most coverage left out scientific experts, public health officials and people with lived experience (p. 2), were not measured in this study, whose coded variables are listed as state, incidents and reference to government guidance. The abstract also says the authors characterized mainstream and social media content, but no social media posts were coded.

timeline.event: DEA statement and video on fentanyl exposure; the first notable surge of coverage coincided with it, and the video appeared in 80 articles (p. 2).

ACMT and AACT position statement, the reference for coding misinformation and for the statement that the reported symptoms are not consistent with opioid toxicity (pp. 1–2); the record moss_2017 has the same title.

Herman et al. (2020): review of media reports of unintentional opioid exposure of first responders, cited alongside this study by Attaway et al. (2021) and del Pozo et al. (2021); not read for this card.
Winograd et al. (2020), with Beletsky as an author: an emergency-responder training with a 10-minute fentanyl segment; answers to a belief item before and immediately after (card sc_winograd_2020).
Attaway et al. (2021) cite this study for media stories that remain uncorrected and are shared thousands of times (p. 2) (card sc_attaway_2021).

del Pozo et al. (2021), with Beletsky and Kang as authors, cite this study for social media posts reaching 70 million viewers or more (p. 2), a figure this study presents as an upper bound on potential views (card sc_del_pozo_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: No other analysis of news coverage and sharing on this question appears in the sources read. Later papers rely on this study for the spread of misinformation (Attaway et al., 2021) or cite its 70-million figure as viewers reached (del Pozo et al., 2021). The study documents the volume and sharing of coverage; it does not test whether that coverage changed beliefs or behaviour.

funding.funder: Research was supported by a grant from the Vital Projects Fund; the funder had no role in the design, implementation or interpretation of the study (Ethics and Acknowledgements, p. 3).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no conflicts of interests to declare (Declarations of Interests, p. 3).
funding.affiliations_note: Four authors, including the corresponding author, are at the Health in Justice Action Lab of Northeastern University (School of Law and College of Health Sciences); the others at the Harvard-MIT Center for Regulatory Science, the Division of Medical Toxicology of University Hospitals Cleveland, the MIT Center for Civic Media, Northeastern's Khoury College of Computer Sciences, UC San Diego and Northeastern's Center for Health Policy and Law (p. 1). The first author is also an author of the two training evaluations on this question (Winograd et al., 2020; del Pozo et al., 2021), and del Pozo et al. name the Health in Justice Action Lab as the home of the SHIELD training they evaluate. Recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A content analysis with a published codebook and inter-rater agreement, a neutral category that separates incident reports from endorsement, complete counts by outlet, state and incident, and measured audience data instead of a multiplier, linked to surveys of first responders and the public to test whether exposure to such coverage predicts the belief.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Media Cloud's online news collections are a reasonable frame for online US news coverage, but paywalls and archiving gaps limit coverage (p. 3), and broadcast news, police bulletins and social media posts are outside the frame.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: A keyword census of the database rather than a sample; the nine-term query was not validated, and the relevance criteria and the number of hits screened are not reported.

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 551 articles; the corrective group is small (45, of which 18 unequivocally corrective), so its share totals depend on few articles.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Period, query, categories and the source of share data are described; outlets, states, incidents and the collections used are not listed, and the Supplement was not available.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 551 relevant articles were coded and their shares counted; the split by national and local outlets does not reconcile by two articles (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Explicit definitions anchored in the ACMT/AACT statement, but misinformation includes reports of anecdotal incidents and there is no neutral category, so the label covers more than endorsement of the risk.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Standardized protocol and four trained coders with redundant coding and adjudication; no inter-rater agreement is reported.

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis
domains.note: Descriptive counts suit the aim, but the reach figures depend on an assumed multiplier and are upper bounds that the abstract presents as people reached; the factor of 15 uses the narrowest comparison; no uncertainty is given.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: No response rate applies; database coverage is considered under items 1 and 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The counts and share totals are probably close to right for what this search retrieved and these coders classified. The limits are an unvalidated search of one database, a misinformation category broad enough to include neutral incident reporting, no reported coder agreement, and reach figures that are modelled upper bounds. Citable for: the authors' coding of 551 articles from January 2015 to September 2019 (506 misinformation, 45 corrective or partially corrective, 18 unequivocally corrective) and their Facebook share totals; the two most-shared incidents as described from news reports. Not citable for: numbers of people reached or persuaded, effects of the coverage or of government statements, or the toxicology of casual contact with fentanyl.

key_findings.finding: Between May and December 2019 the authors searched Media Cloud for articles published January 2015 to September 2019 with nine terms on casual fentanyl exposure (fentanyl AND glove*, mask*, touch*, contact*, absor*, inhal*, breath* or expos*), then reviewed the results for relevance and duplication.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Articles were coded misinformation (endorsing overdose risk from casual touch or inhalation, or presenting anecdotal accounts mentioning its rumoured sequelae), corrective (accurately stating the lack of immediate risk or debunking it) or partially corrective (both), by four trained reviewers with redundant coding and staff resolution of discordant codes; reach was modelled from Facebook shares (CrowdTangle) multiplied by 155 contacts, as an upper bound on views.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The queries produced 551 relevant articles (47 national, 504 from state and local sources), January 2015 to September 2019, spanning 48 states, most from Texas and Pennsylvania.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 506 articles (92%) contained misinformation, 37 of them in national outlets; misinformation received 450,011 Facebook shares, with an upper bound of 69,751,705 potential views, which the authors distinguish from unique viewers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 45 articles (8 in national outlets) were corrective or partially corrective, 8% of the dataset, with 48,235 Facebook shares, roughly one-tenth of the shares of misinformation; only 18 were unequivocally corrective, with 29,652 shares (printed as 6.6% of total) and a potential reach of 4,596,060 views.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: 6.6% equals 29,652/450,011, the ratio to misinformation shares; of all 498,246 shares it is 6.0% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The first notable surge of coverage coincided with a 2016 DEA statement that a small amount of fentanyl ingested or absorbed through the skin can kill; its video, in which two Atlantic County, New Jersey officers describe an overdose after inhaling airborne fentanyl with symptoms the authors, citing ACMT 2017, call consistent with panic attacks, appeared in 80 articles.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (starts left column, continues right column)

key_findings.finding: The most-shared story (133,751 Facebook shares across 25 states; nearly 21,000,000 potential views) concerned an East Liverpool, Ohio officer who said he felt his body shutting down after brushing white powder off his uniform after a 2017 traffic stop and received four doses of naloxone; neither the powder's composition nor his overdose was confirmed by laboratory testing. The next (45,533 shares; about 7,000,000 potential views) concerned a Columbus, Ohio officer who inhaled what he thought was fentanyl, later confirmed as methamphetamine; some articles were updated but did not meaningfully correct the record.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The incident outcomes are the authors' summaries of news reports (Moshtaghian, 2017; a 2018 local television report), not the authors' own verification.

key_findings.finding: The abstract reports approximately 450,000 shares potentially reaching nearly 70,000,000 people on Facebook from 2015 to 2019, and excess visibility of misinformation by a factor of 15 compared with corrective content, which had fewer than 30,000 shares and a potential reach of 4,600,000.

key_findings.note: The factor of 15 and the 30,000 and 4,600,000 figures refer to the 18 unequivocally corrective articles only; the Results call the reach figures upper bounds on views, not unique viewers (p. 2).
