design_detail: Short report (Health & Justice 9, article 34): single-group before-and-after evaluation, filed as a prospective cohort, of the SHIELD (Safety and Health Integration in the Enforcement of Laws on Drugs) training for law enforcement in Indiana. Three 3-hour sessions were held by Zoom in December 2020, March 2021 and June 2021, facilitated by the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy and led by a former police officer; they covered needle-stick injuries, officer mental health, the public safety benefits of harm reduction programmes and addiction treatment, and a 10-minute module on fentanyl exposure. Of 204 attendees from 49 Indiana counties, 129 completed a baseline survey immediately before the training and 69 completed a follow-up survey that could be linked to their baseline by a code derived from name and date of birth. One item, rated on a 6-point scale (1 = strongly agree to 6 = strongly disagree), asked whether first responders who encounter fentanyl “are at great risk of overdose by touching it or inhaling it”. Analyses: descriptive statistics, chi-square, ANOVA, and independent and paired t-tests (SPSS). Appraised with ROBINS-I, as for sc_winograd_2020 and sc_park_2020. Tables 1 and 2 have no text layer and were read from the rendered pages.
can_establish: How many of 129 Indiana officers attending a SHIELD training agreed, before it, that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, and how the 69 who completed the linked follow-up answered afterwards.
cannot_establish: Whether the training, let alone its 10-minute module, caused the change (no comparison group, and the follow-up came after the corrective message), whether the change lasted or altered behaviour, or how the 135 attendees without a follow-up survey would have answered; nor anything about the actual risk of touching or inhaling fentanyl.

sample.recruitment: Law enforcement officials attending SHIELD trainings facilitated by the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy, from 49 Indiana counties (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Whether attendance was voluntary or assigned is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond attendance. Roles at baseline included patrol, administration, community corrections, detective, community affairs or outreach, narcotics and other (Table 1, p. 3).
sample.demographics: Baseline, n = 129 (Table 1, p. 3): mean age 45.1 (SD 10.7); 97 male (75.2%), 32 female (24.8%); 109 White (84.5%), 10 Black (7.8%), 6 Hispanic (4.7%), 4 other (3.1%); education high school 16, some college 30, associate's degree 17, bachelor's degree 49 (38.0%), post-baccalaureate degree 17; 27 (20.9%) with 0–3 years in law enforcement and 29 (22.5%) with more than 25; patrol 40 (31.0%), administration 32 (24.8%), community corrections 16 (12.4%); prior fentanyl exposure training 79 (61.2%). Follow-up completers, n = 69: mean age 45.1 (SD 10.7); 51 male (73.9%); 58 White (84.1%); 32 with a bachelor's degree (46.4%) and 5 with high school only (7.2%); 23 patrol (33.3%); 46 with prior fentanyl exposure training (66.7%).
sample.attrition: 129 of 204 attendees (63.2%) completed the baseline survey and 69 of the 129 (53.5%) the follow-up, 34% of attendees overall (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2; Abstract, p. 1). The authors report no significant demographic differences between completers and baseline-only respondents (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 4); baseline belief is not compared, although the completers' baseline mean (2.2) was close to that of all 129 (2.3).
sample.selection_effects: Attendees of one state's training programme during the COVID-19 pandemic, with about a third of attendees in the pre–post comparison. Completers more often held a bachelor's degree (46.4% vs 38.0%) and less often had high school only (7.2% vs 12.4%) than all baseline respondents (Table 1). Over half had prior fentanyl exposure precaution training, which the authors characterize as the misinformation the module corrects (p. 3); its content was not assessed.

exposure.measurement: Attendance at one 3-hour SHIELD session by Zoom (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2). The fentanyl module emphasized that a nicotine transdermal patch is specially formulated to promote absorption through the skin, an effect that exposing skin to tobacco cannot achieve, and that the same principle applies to fentanyl; that people routinely process and package illicit fentanyl in large quantities in confined spaces without reported transdermal or inhalation overdoses or evidence of precautions; and that false beliefs about fentanyl's lethality can produce physical reactions consistent with severe panic, which are inconsistent with exposure to fentanyl (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses: one 3-hour session with a 10-minute fentanyl module.

comparison.controls: None: single-group pre–post among the 69 linked respondents; baseline comparisons by respondent characteristics among the 129.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Without a comparison group, the change cannot be separated from answering the item a second time, from demand characteristics after a corrective message, or from the remaining 170 minutes of training. The content of officers' prior fentanyl training and their media exposure were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: One item on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 2 = agree, 3 = somewhat agree, 4 = somewhat disagree, 5 = disagree, 6 = strongly disagree) on whether first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching it or inhaling it (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 2; Table 2 note, p. 4). The baseline survey was given during time allotted at the start of the training; the follow-up was online.
outcomes.validity_norms: Single unvalidated item that combines two routes (touching or inhaling) and a degree (great risk), so disagreement may concern the degree of risk rather than any risk.
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement: strongly agree, agree or somewhat agree; disagreement: the three disagree options. Change: the paired difference in mean score among the 69.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: baseline comparisons by education, role, age, race, gender, length of service and prior training, the same comparisons at follow-up, and the paired test, all at p < .05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Baseline, n = 129 (Table 2, p. 4): 52 strongly agree, 42 agree, 9 somewhat agree, 6 somewhat disagree, 8 disagree, 12 strongly disagree; 103 agreed (79.8%) and 26 disagreed (20.2%); mean 2.3 (SD 1.6). Follow-up, n = 69: 9, 8, 10, 8, 12 and 22 respectively; 27 agreed (39.1%) and 42 disagreed (60.9%); mean 4.0 (SD 1.8). Paired t-test among the 69: mean 2.2 to 4.0, t = 6.52, p < .001, with a printed 95% CI [1.05, 0.51] and Cohen's d = 2.33. At baseline, respondents with a college degree (n = 83) scored 2.5 against 1.9 for those without (t = 2.17, printed 95% CI [1.14, 0.05], printed Cohen's d = 2.33, p = .032); role differed (F = 2.71, p = .017), patrol against others 2.6 against 1.8 (t = 2.95, 95% CI [0.26, 1.32], printed Cohen's d = 1.61, p = .004); no differences by age, race, gender, length of service or prior fentanyl-related training (Results, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 4). Editors' calculations: Wilson 95% CIs 72.1 to 85.9% for baseline agreement and 28.5 to 50.9% for follow-up agreement; standardized effects recomputed from t and n are about d = 0.40 (degree, 83 vs 46), d = 0.56 (patrol, 40 vs 89) and d_z = 0.78 (paired, n = 69); the 95% CI for the paired mean change of 1.8 points is about 1.25 to 2.35. The printed paired interval [0.51, 1.05] matches the interval for d_z (about 0.52 to 1.05), and the printed 2.33 matches the SD of the paired differences (about 2.3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study is presented as confirming the findings of an earlier pilot (Winograd et al., 2020) (Discussion, p. 4). Approved as exempt by the Wayne State University IRB as a minimal-risk training evaluation (#2020037) (pp. 2, 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: The completers' baseline answers are given only as a mean (2.2), not as percentages, so the abstract's comparison of 79.8% (of 129) with 39.1% (of 69) mixes denominators.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors say 69 respondents is a small number that limits confidence in the conclusions (p. 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Before a 3-hour SHIELD training, 103 of 129 Indiana officers (79.8%) agreed that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, 52 of them strongly. Of the 69 who completed the linked follow-up, 27 (39.1%) still agreed and 22 strongly disagreed; their mean score moved from 2.2 to 4.0 on the 6-point scale (t = 6.52; d_z about 0.8 by editors' calculation). Two-thirds of attendees are missing from the pre–post comparison, and there was no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes a “10-min online training” (p. 1), whereas the Methods describe a 10-minute module within a 3-hour training that also covered needle-stick injuries, officer mental health, harm reduction and treatment (p. 2). The abstract sets 79.8% at baseline (of 129) against 39.1% at follow-up (of 69) with p < .001, a p-value that comes from the paired t-test on the means of 69. The Discussion says the analysis “confirms that a brief training module” had a corrective effect and that the intervention had a “considerable effect” (p. 4), relying on printed effect sizes that do not match the data (see reporting issues), and suggests that a training video with similar content shown at roll calls holds promise, although no video was tested. The authors acknowledge the low follow-up response, that knowledge rather than behaviour was measured and that persistence was not examined (pp. 4–5), but argue that the attrition does not necessarily indicate non-response bias, on the basis of demographic comparisons only.

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT joint report, cited in its Clinical Toxicology printing (Moss et al., 2018) for very low risk from incidental transdermal exposure and for 200 minutes of breathing fentanyl at the highest airborne concentrations being needed to reach a therapeutic dose (p. 2); the record moss_2017 has the same title.
Persaud and Jennings (2020): survey of New York first responders, cited as finding that 80% believed briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (p. 2); not read.

Winograd et al. (2020), the pilot this study sets out to confirm, with two of the same authors: after a training with a 10-minute segment, the share of 140 Missouri responders answering False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl rose from 20.9% to 83.6% (card sc_winograd_2020). This paper describes those figures as concerning 113 officers (p. 2).

Beletsky et al. (2020), with two of the same authors, cited for social media posts reaching 70 million viewers or more (p. 2), a figure that study presents as an upper bound on potential views (card sc_beletsky_2020).
Herman et al. (2020), cited for no reported exposure incident having been confirmed as an overdose (p. 2); not read for this card.
Attaway et al. (2021), cited for misinformation spreading through policing networks and the need for corrective messaging (pp. 1–2) (card sc_attaway_2021).
This study published (received 10 September, published online 24 November 2021).

replication.where_it_stands: Two uncontrolled before-and-after studies by overlapping teams (Winograd et al., 2020; this study) found that first responders' agreement with the belief fell after a training that included a short fentanyl module, measured at or soon after the training with different single items. No controlled evaluation, delayed follow-up or behavioural outcome appears in the sources read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I asks whether the study can estimate the effect of the training on officers' belief. It cannot: there is no comparison group, two-thirds of attendees are missing from the pre–post comparison, the outcome is one double-barrelled item answered after the corrective message, and the printed effect sizes are wrong. Citable for: the share of these Indiana officers agreeing with the statement before training (103 of 129, 79.8%) and the answers of the 69 who completed the follow-up (27 still agreeing, 39.1%). Not citable for: the size or persistence of a training effect, the effect of the 10-minute module alone, or behaviour.

design_detail: Brief report (Harm Reduct J 17, article 58): single-group before-and-after evaluation, filed as a prospective cohort, of an overdose education and response training for emergency responders in the Eastern Region of Missouri. Between January and August 2019 project staff ran eight law enforcement and three EMS trainings reaching 200 participants; 140 were analysed (113 law enforcement or security officers, the LEO group; 27 EMS, EMT or fire department workers, the EMS group). The training, about 2 hours long, covered addiction, harm reduction, naloxone-related risk compensation, treatment medications and Missouri's naloxone and Good Samaritan laws, and included about 10 minutes on the medical impossibility of overdose from incidental skin contact with fentanyl, taught by an emergency medicine physician in LEO trainings and by the project manager in EMS trainings. A paper survey was completed just before and immediately after the training; only one True/False item was analysed. Differences between professions were tested with Fisher's exact test and pre–post change with McNemar's test. Appraised with ROBINS-I because the training is an intervention and the paper infers its effect, as for sc_park_2020.
can_establish: How these 140 Missouri emergency responders answered True or False to “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.” just before and immediately after a training that included a 10-minute corrective segment, overall and by profession.
cannot_establish: Whether the training caused a lasting change of belief (no comparison group, and the same item was answered again immediately after the trainer had given the answer), whether the 10-minute segment alone produced it (it was part of a 2-hour training), whether responders acted differently at overdose scenes, or anything about the actual risk of touching fentanyl.

sample.recruitment: Attendees of 11 trainings (8 for law enforcement, 3 for EMS) run by project staff in the Eastern Region of Missouri, January to August 2019, as part of a broader effort to improve community access to naloxone (Introduction, last paragraph, and Methods › Participants, p. 2). How agencies and attendees came to the trainings is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Trainings were tailored for professional emergency responders; other professionals could attend, but their surveys were omitted (n = 17) (Methods › Participants, p. 2). No other criteria are stated, and whether the analysis required both surveys is not stated.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 3), N = 140: mean age 40.96 (SD 11.27); 110 men (printed 79.7%); 115 White (82.1%), 15 Black (10.7%), 4 multiracial or other (2.9%), 6 refused (4.3%); 5 Hispanic or Latino(a) (3.6%). LEO group (n = 113): mean age 40.6 (SD 11.0), 98 men (86.7%), 89 White (78.8%), 15 Black (13.3%). EMS group (n = 27): mean age 42.3 (SD 12.5), 12 men (44.4%), 26 White (96.3%).
sample.attrition: 200 participants were reached; 17 other professionals were omitted and 140 analysed, leaving 43 (21.5% of 200) unaccounted for (editors' subtraction; the paper does not explain them). The number with both a pre and a post survey is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One region of one state; responders were predominantly White and male, which the authors name as a limit to generalizability (p. 4); the LEO group includes security officers; the EMS group is small (27). The 43 unexplained participants may include people who missed one of the two surveys.

exposure.measurement: Everyone analysed attended the training (Methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Its content: addiction as a chronic brain disease, harm reduction principles, concerns about enabling drug use (naloxone-related risk compensation), addiction treatment medications, Missouri's naloxone and Good Samaritan laws, and accurate information on the medical impossibility of overdosing from incidental skin exposure to fentanyl, which took about 10 minutes to present and discuss. The fentanyl segment was taught by an emergency medicine physician in LEO trainings and by the project manager in EMS trainings. The whole training lasted about 2 hours (Limitations and future directions, p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses: one session of about 2 hours, with about 10 minutes on fentanyl contact.

comparison.controls: None: single-group pre–post. The LEO and EMS groups were compared with each other at each time point (Fisher's exact test).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: With no comparison group and an immediate post-test, the change cannot be separated from answering the same item twice, from wanting to give the answer just taught (demand characteristics) or from the other modules of the training; the two professions also had different presenters (physician or project manager). Prior fentanyl training and media exposure were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: One original item, answered True or False before and after the training: “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.” (Methods › Measure of belief in fentanyl exposure risk, p. 2). The paper survey also had items on overdose recognition and response, which were not analysed in this paper (Procedure, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). Surveys were later entered into REDCap by a research assistant.
outcomes.validity_norms: Single unvalidated item; no reliability or validity data.
outcomes.operationalization: Correct answer: False. Outcome: the proportion answering False before and after the training.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; five tests on the one item (two Fisher's exact tests, three McNemar's tests). Other survey items were not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed paper survey). How the pre and post surveys were linked for the paired analysis, and whether they were anonymous, is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages and p-values only (Results, pp. 2–3; Fig. 1, p. 3). Before training, 20.9% of all participants answered False; LEO 16.8%, EMS 37.0% (Fisher's exact p = .033). After training, 83.6% answered False (a 62.7-point difference; McNemar's p < .001); LEO 81.4% and EMS 92.6% (each McNemar's p < .001), increases of 64.6 and 55.6 points; the professions did not differ significantly after training (Fisher's p = .301). Editors' calculations from the group percentages and sizes: LEO 19/113 before and 92/113 after, EMS 10/27 and 25/27, all 29/140 (20.7%) and 117/140 (83.6%). Wilson 95% CIs: all participants 14.8 to 28.2% before and 76.6 to 88.8% after; LEO after 73.3 to 87.5%; EMS after 76.6 to 97.9%. Discordant pairs are not reported; at least 88 people must have changed from True to False. Two-sided Fisher's exact p recomputed from these counts: 0.032 before (matches the printed .033) and 0.25 after (printed .301).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. Approved by the University of Missouri–St. Louis IRB (registration number 00000756); consent forms were signed before the pre-training survey (Ethics approval and consent to participate, p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the fentanyl item of a multi-item survey is analysed, which the authors state (p. 2). The number answering each survey, the paired n and the discordant counts are not given.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors note the relatively small sample (p. 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Just before training, about four in five of these Missouri responders did not answer False to the statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl (20.9% answered False; 16.8% of the LEO group and 37.0% of the EMS group). Immediately after a 2-hour training with a 10-minute corrective segment, 83.6% answered False (LEO 81.4%, EMS 92.6%). There was no comparison group and no later follow-up, and 140 of 200 participants were analysed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the authors determined that the 10-minute presentation “reduces emergency responders' endorsement of the belief they could overdose” (p. 3); the Conclusions call the study the “first to demonstrate the effectiveness of a training intervention” (p. 4); the title speaks of early evidence of success. The Limitations, however, say the simple design prevented assessing confounding or drawing causal inferences, and that the 2-hour training included other modules, so whether a brief fentanyl-focused training suffices remains to be studied (p. 4). The non-significant post-training difference between professions (p = .301, with 27 in the EMS group) is read as the difference going away, and the pre-training difference is attributed, without data, to EMS personnel's medical training and less contact with police and DEA colleagues (p. 3). Answers given immediately after the trainer stated the correct answer show what participants reported then, not a lasting change of belief or behaviour; the authors acknowledge that behaviour was not linked (p. 4). The Introduction's statement that overdose from incidental skin contact is a medical impossibility cites two press articles, one of them a newspaper opinion piece, followed by the ACMT/AACT statement and a NIOSH database entry for the claim having been debunked (p. 1; references 14–16 and 26, p. 5); the study measures belief, not risk.

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement, cited in its Clinical Toxicology printing (Moss et al., 2018) as officially debunking overdose from incidental contact (p. 1); the record moss_2017 has the same title.

Persaud and Jennings (2019): survey of 247 New York first responders, cited as finding that 80% believed briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, and as the only earlier study of responders' perceptions (p. 2); not read.
Herman et al. (2020), cited for over 150 media reports of first responder exposures to opioids in 2017 (p. 1); not read for this card.
This study published (received 27 May, published online 24 August 2020).
Attaway et al. (2021) cite this study for a brief presentation reducing responders' belief that they could overdose from contact (p. 5) (card sc_attaway_2021).

del Pozo et al. (2021), with two of the same authors (Goulka, Beletsky), set out to confirm this study among Indiana officers: agreement with a different 6-point item fell from 79.8% of 129 at baseline to 39.1% of 69 at follow-up. They describe this study's 20.9% to 83.6% as concerning 113 officers, although those figures are for all 140 responders (card sc_del_pozo_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: One further uncontrolled before-and-after study, by an overlapping team with a different item, found change in the same direction, smaller and with heavy attrition (del Pozo et al., 2021). No controlled or randomized evaluation, delayed follow-up or behavioural outcome appears in the sources read; the authors call for testing a stand-alone fentanyl-focused training and for linking beliefs to behaviour (p. 4).

funding.funder: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, through the Prescription Drug Overdose (PDO) Grant 1H79SP022118 awarded to the Missouri Department of Mental Health; the work was funded wholly or in part by the Missouri Department of Mental Health on behalf of the University of Missouri, St. Louis, and does not necessarily reflect the views of either agency (Funding, p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Competing interests, p. 4).
funding.affiliations_note: Missouri Institute of Mental Health, University of Missouri–St. Louis (four authors); National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Abuse, St. Louis; Northeastern University (Goulka, Beletsky), whose authors also wrote Beletsky et al. (2020) and del Pozo et al. (2021). The authors state that they developed the training evaluated (p. 2), so this is a developer-led evaluation. Recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial in which training sessions or agencies receive the standard overdose training with or without the fentanyl segment (or the segment against an attention control), measured with a validated multi-item scale that separates touching from inhaling, at a delayed follow-up of weeks to months with complete paired data, and with recorded behaviour at overdose scenes (time to naloxone, protective equipment, calls for hazmat teams).

domains.domain: Bias due to confounding
domains.note: No comparison group: the immediate pre–post change cannot be separated from answering the item a second time, from demand characteristics just after the trainer gave the answer, or from the rest of the 2-hour training. The comparison between professions is also confounded by presenter.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Attendees of trainings in one region, selection of agencies and attendees not described; 140 of 200 participants analysed, 43 of them unexplained.

domains.domain: Bias in classification of interventions
domains.note: Everyone analysed attended the training. The intervention received is the whole 2-hour training, not the 10-minute segment that the Discussion names.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Content was tailored to the audience and the fentanyl segment was delivered by different presenters for the two professions; fidelity was not recorded.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing data
domains.note: 43 participants (21.5%) are unaccounted for; the paired n is not reported, and the overall pre-training percentage implies a different denominator from the group figures.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of outcomes
domains.note: One unvalidated True/False item, self-completed in the training room immediately after the correct answer had been taught; respondents knew what the training wanted them to answer.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Only one item of a multi-item survey is reported, although it is the stated aim; paired counts are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I asks whether the study can estimate the effect of the training on belief. It cannot: there is no comparison group, the post-test came immediately after the answer was taught, the outcome is one self-completed item, and 43 participants are unexplained. Citable for: how common the belief was among these Missouri responders before training (20.9% answered False to “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.”; LEO 16.8%, EMS 37.0%) and what they answered immediately afterwards (83.6% False). Not citable for: a lasting or causal change in belief, the effect of the 10-minute segment alone, or any change in behaviour.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 110 men as 79.7% of the overall sample of 140, while the group percentages use the full 113 and 27; by the editors' calculation 110/140 = 78.6%, and 79.7% fits a denominator of 138.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; denominators are inconsistent within the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The post-training comparison of professions is printed as Fisher's exact p = .301, from 81.4% of 113 and 92.6% of 27 answering False; in the editors' recomputation from those proportions (92/113 vs 25/27) the two-sided p is 0.25, while the pre-training p (.033) reproduces as 0.032.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods use McNemar's test for paired data but do not say how pre and post surveys were linked or how many pairs there were, and give no discordant counts; the ethics statement refers to each pre and/or post-training test, implying that some participants completed only one.

design_detail: NIOSH case series: a journal article summarizing two Health Hazard Evaluations (HHE 1 and HHE 2) of incidents in two US states in 2017 and 2018 in which five police officers became ill during or soon after responses involving illicit drugs. Retrospective: site visits at each agency with interviews of the officers who had symptoms and of others (number not given), held weeks to months after the incidents; review of medical records, agency documentation of the incidents and the forensic laboratory's results for evidence samples; body-camera footage in HHE 2 only (PDF pp. 1–3, 8). Nothing was sampled in the air, on surfaces or on skin; the only biological tests were those the emergency departments chose to do (none for the officer in HHE 1; urine drug screens for the four officers in HHE 2 and blood tests for three of them). One figure (a photograph of materials found in HHE 1), Table 1 (each officer's activities, symptoms, onset and the emergency physician's clinical impression) and Table 2 (substances identified by the forensic laboratory, with weights). No statistics. The article does not say which incident happened in which year or state; its references 10 and 11 are the two evaluation reports, a New Hampshire report on one officer (NIOSH HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and a Virginia report on officers (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018), so HHE 1, with one officer, is probably the New Hampshire incident (editors' inference from the report titles; PDF p. 11). Neither incident is the one in NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (card sc_niosh_2018: two officers, powder from a locked metal box blown into their faces, no opioid identified), which has another number, differs in every detail and is not cited in this article.
can_establish: What happened to five officers in two incidents, as reconstructed from records, interviews and, in one incident, body-camera footage: the circumstances, the symptoms and when they began, the clinical findings and the emergency physicians' impressions, the limited testing of the officers, and the drugs the forensic laboratory identified in evidence from each scene; and the NIOSH authors' interpretation and their views on prevention.
cannot_establish: Whether any officer took in any drug, by which route or in what amount, or what caused the symptoms (opioids, stimulants, other substances, anxiety or perceived risk, or another condition): nothing was measured on the officers or around them, no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl or synthetic cathinones, one officer had no test at all, and perceived risk was not assessed; nor how often responders who meet drugs become ill, since two referred incidents were chosen to illustrate scenarios.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: two incidents for which law enforcement agencies requested NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations of officers' health effects after unintentional exposure to drugs (PDF pp. 2–3), chosen by the authors to illustrate different scenarios that might lead to exposure and health effects (PDF p. 5). The five officers who had symptoms were interviewed, as were others (PDF p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable. How many NIOSH evaluations the two incidents were chosen from is not stated; other evaluations are only pointed to on a NIOSH web page (PDF p. 5).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex, years of service or medical history for any officer. As context only, the introduction cites an estimated 701,000 sworn full-time officers in about 15,300 US agencies in 2016 (PDF p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: Incidents reached NIOSH because officers became ill and their agency asked for an evaluation, and the authors then chose two to illustrate scenarios; incidents without symptoms, or not referred, are not represented. Nothing follows about how often responders who meet drugs become ill, or about how many incidents would show a confirmed exposure if tested.

exposure.measurement: Not measured. HHE 1 (PDF p. 3): during a traffic stop and vehicle search, a gust of wind blew powder from an unlabelled rubber container, opened outside the vehicle, onto the officer, who said the powder was all over the officer and the uniform; the officer wore a short-sleeved uniform and no gloves, brushed the powder off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer; emergency medical service (EMS) staff later washed the exposed skin with water. HHE 2 (PDF p. 4): three officers entered a hotel room where drug paraphernalia and powders lay in plain view and the toilet had been heard flushing many times; they wore short sleeves, two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after, and they took turns to fetch and put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen; one of them later worked at headquarters on a computer and with a camera used in the room, and a fourth officer, who never entered the room, handled that camera and other items from the room, which had no visible contamination, and cleaned gear and a vehicle (Table 1, PDF p. 15). All four were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing) before going to hospital. No air, surface, skin or blood sampling.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Unknown amounts of material of unknown concentration. The authors consider breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing, absorption through the skin, or a combination, all possible in both incidents (PDF p. 6). HHE 1 was outdoors in hot, windy weather; HHE 2 was indoors, beside a bathroom where repeated flushing may have contaminated surfaces (PDF p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: Forensic laboratory results for evidence from the scenes (Table 2, PDF p. 16), with weights but no concentrations or purities: HHE 1, fentanyl (compressed tan powder, 9.98 g), fentanyl with methamphetamine (tan powder and chunks, 1.56 g: the rubber container the officer opened), methamphetamine (crystals, 0.006 g) and buprenorphine (sealed packages labelled as a sublingual film; one package tested); HHE 2, dibutylone (residue), N-ethylpentylone (powder, solid material and residue, 2.87 g), heroin (powder, 0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl (residue), cocaine and methamphetamine (residue, and liquid in a syringe) and fentanyl (powder and residue, 0.14 g). The Results call the HHE 2 findings opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones (PDF p. 5). The authors note that not every substance at a scene may be sent to the laboratory (PDF p. 6).

comparison.controls: None. The authors set the officers' findings against the textbook signs of severe opioid toxicity (profound lethargy or other depression of the central nervous system; shallow, slow or absent breathing; constricted pupils; slow heart rate; low body temperature) and of stimulant toxicity (PDF p. 5). Others present (the second officer in HHE 1; the two people detained in HHE 2) are not compared.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical histories, anxiety and perceived risk are not reported; the authors say perceived risk was not assessed (PDF p. 6) and that medical conditions not evaluated in the emergency department could not be assessed afterwards (PDF p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Symptoms as the officers reported them; EMS and emergency department records (vital signs, pupils, mental status, electrocardiograms; blood tests for three officers in HHE 2; urine drug screens for the four officers in HHE 2); the emergency physicians' clinical impressions (Table 1, PDF p. 15); the forensic laboratory's identification of evidence samples (Table 2, PDF p. 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: For the HHE 1 officer, vital signs are set against normal values stated in the text (blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg or above defined as abnormal; resting breathing rate 12 to 15 a minute; heart rate under 100; pupils 2 to 4 mm depending on light; PDF p. 3). The urine screens used standard cut-offs (amphetamines 500 ng/mL, cocaine 150 ng/mL); the opiate screen does not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, and most amphetamine screens do not readily detect synthetic cathinones (PDF p. 7). There is no exposure biomarker.
outcomes.operationalization: Health effects are the symptoms that kept the officers from their duties; opioid toxicity is judged clinically against the signs of severe toxicity; exposure is inferred from the circumstances and from what the laboratory identified at the scene, not measured.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The investigators and the clinicians knew the circumstances; the emergency physicians' impressions name possible fentanyl exposure for three officers and possible accidental overdose for one (Table 1).

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics: a narrative account of five officers in two incidents. The numbers reported are the HHE 1 officer's vital signs and timings (PDF p. 3), one HHE 2 officer's emergency department breathing rate of 9 to 20 a minute (PDF p. 4), the onset times in Table 1 (PDF p. 15), the urine screen cut-offs (PDF p. 7) and the evidence weights in Table 2 (PDF p. 16).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Health Hazard Evaluations are done at an employer's request; no protocol is mentioned. Ethics review was judged unnecessary because the evaluations were considered a public health activity; written consent was obtained for the release of medical records (PDF p. 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Vital signs are given as values for the HHE 1 officer but mostly as categories for the HHE 2 officers; when the urine samples were taken, relative to the incident, is not given; which incident happened in which year and state is not stated; the forensic laboratory's methods and detection limits are not given; and the number of NIOSH evaluations from which the two incidents were chosen is not stated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Five officers in two incidents reported non-specific symptoms (disorientation, lightheadedness or dizziness, blurry vision, weakness, warmth, sweating, numbness of both hands and the tongue, headache, feeling drunk, high, groggy or sleepy), beginning within 5 minutes in HHE 1 and about 25 to 90 minutes after the response began in HHE 2; one officer slumped to the ground and improved rapidly after a colleague gave one dose of intranasal naloxone. No officer was reported to have depressed breathing; in the emergency department all were alert, none had documented constricted pupils and the electrocardiograms were normal; blood pressure and heart rate were normal to raised, and one officer's breathing rate ranged from 9 to 20 a minute. No officer had a test able to detect fentanyl: the HHE 1 officer had no laboratory test, and the urine screens of the four HHE 2 officers, which cannot detect fentanyl, were negative for every drug class screened. The laboratory identified fentanyl, with methamphetamine, in the powder left in the container that blew onto the HHE 1 officer, and fentanyl, a fentanyl analogue, heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones in evidence from the hotel room.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors' main conclusion is hedged: the effects were not consistent with severe, life-threatening opioid toxicity, the risks cannot yet be characterized with certainty, and timely prospective toxicological evaluation of affected responders is needed (PDF pp. 1–2, 5, 10). In places the article goes further than its data: the abstract describes the officers as exposed to opioid and stimulant drugs (PDF p. 1), which nothing measured on the officers shows; the Discussion takes one officer's improvement after naloxone as suggesting that opioids were a substantial component of the mixed exposure (PDF p. 5), from one uncontrolled observation in an officer who had no blood test and whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; it lists nausea among the symptoms the officers reported (PDF p. 5), though nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms (PDF pp. 3–4; Table 1, PDF p. 15); and the prevention section says the potential for risk is clear from these investigations and warns against treating the effects as merely a reflection of perceived risk (PDF p. 8), although perceived risk was not assessed (PDF p. 6).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, cited here (reference 30, given as published in Clinical Toxicology) with two other sources for the statement that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible contamination is promptly removed (PDF pp. 6, 12).

The two NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation reports summarized here: New Hampshire (HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and Virginia (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018), both by Chiu, Hornsby-Myers and Trout (references 10 and 11, PDF p. 11); not read.

NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (November 2018), by Jackson, Chiu and Hornsby-Myers: a different incident (two officers, powder from a locked metal box blown into their faces, no opioid identified in the seized items); not cited in this article, whose web references were accessed in October 2018.

Herman et al. cite this article (their reference 9) as a rare case report in which clinical manifestations were not consistent with opioids and none of the officers tested was positive for opioid metabolites (Herman et al., p. 112). The article reports two incidents with five officers; it judges the effects not consistent with severe opioid toxicity while suggesting milder opioid effects and a substantial opioid part for one officer; and its urine screens, negative for opiates, could not detect fentanyl, while one officer had no test (PDF pp. 3–5, 7).

replication.where_it_stands: Two more incidents investigated by NIOSH, written up by authors who also wrote the NIOSH report on file (sc_niosh_2018), in which officers had non-specific symptoms, no objective signs of severe opioid toxicity were recorded, and exposure was never measured; in neither incident was poisoning confirmed or excluded by a test able to detect fentanyl. The authors call for timely prospective toxicological evaluation of affected responders (PDF pp. 2, 9–10); no such study is on file.

funding.funder: None: the authors report no funding source for the work or the preparation of the article (PDF p. 10). The evaluations were done by NIOSH under its Health Hazard Evaluation program (PDF pp. 2, 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (PDF p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are at NIOSH (PDF p. 1), which also issues the fentanyl guidance for emergency responders that the article supports (reference 14, PDF p. 11). Two authors (Chiu, Hornsby-Myers) are also authors of the NIOSH report on file (niosh_2018), so the two sources are not independent. A disclaimer says the findings are the authors' own and do not necessarily represent the views of NIOSH, CDC or the US Department of Health and Human Services (PDF p. 1). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective, protocol-driven investigation of responders who report symptoms after a suspected exposure: blood and urine taken within minutes to hours and analysed by mass spectrometry for fentanyl, its analogues, stimulants and synthetic cathinones; the material contacted collected and quantified, with air, surface and skin-wipe samples; objective signs (breathing rate, oxygen saturation, pupil size, level of consciousness) recorded at first contact; perceived risk and anxiety measured with validated tools; and responders at the same scenes without symptoms as a comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case reports and small case series without a comparison; most items do not apply to two incidents. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any conclusion about cause, because no exposure was measured, no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl, and the incidents were chosen to illustrate scenarios. The article may be cited, attributed to its NIOSH authors, for: the incidents as reconstructed; the clinical findings recorded, which showed no objective signs of severe opioid toxicity; the absence of any test able to detect fentanyl in the officers; the forensic laboratory's identifications at the scenes; and the authors' statements, including that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder is not expected to be toxic if visible contamination is promptly removed. It may not be cited as a case of confirmed opioid poisoning, as evidence of absorption through the skin, as evidence that the symptoms came from anxiety (not assessed), or for how often such incidents happen.

key_findings.finding: Two NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluations, requested by law enforcement agencies, of incidents in two states in 2017 and 2018: NIOSH staff visited each agency, interviewed the officers who had health effects and others, and reviewed medical records, the agencies' documentation of the incident and forensic laboratory results for evidence samples; body-camera footage was available and reviewed only in HHE 2. The interviews took place weeks to months after the incidents.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2, continued on p. 3) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Investigation Limitations, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The two incidents were chosen to illustrate different types of scenarios that might lead to exposure and health effects; other NIOSH evaluations of responders' exposures are pointed to on a web page. The article's references for the two evaluations are a New Hampshire report on one officer (HETA No. 2018-0132-3322, August 2018) and a Virginia report on officers (HETA No. 2018-0113-3325, September 2018).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 5); references 10 and 11 (PDF p. 11)
key_findings.note: Which incident happened in which year and state is not stated; the report titles suggest that HHE 1 (one officer) is the New Hampshire evaluation. Neither is NIOSH HHE Report No. 2018-0118-3331 (card sc_niosh_2018), which this article does not cite.

key_findings.finding: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, an officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported that it was all over the officer and the uniform; the officer tried to brush it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer reported intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The HHE 1 officer reached the emergency department about 42 minutes after onset, reported mild blurry vision that resolved after several hours, was alert and had no constricted pupils; during transport and the visit the heart rate was 80–85 a minute, the breathing rate 15–21 a minute and the blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104 mmHg; no laboratory tests were done; the symptoms resolved, and the discharge assessment was chemical exposure. The forensic laboratory identified fentanyl and methamphetamine in the powder left in the container (1.56 g) and fentanyl in a compressed tan powder (9.98 g); the Figure 1 legend says material in a paper wrapper beside the container contained fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 1, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 3, continued on p. 4); Figure 1 legend (PDF p. 14); Table 2 and its footnotes (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: HHE 2: four officers became ill during a response to a 911 call about an unconscious person with a possible overdose in a hotel room. Three entered, saw drug paraphernalia and powders scattered in plain view and heard the toilet flushed many times; the person was intoxicated but conscious and refused care. They wore short sleeves; two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after; they took turns to put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen. One went back to headquarters to process a search warrant, using a computer and a camera used in the room; a fourth officer, who did not enter the room, helped there, handling the camera and other items from the room that had no visible contamination.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: At headquarters both officers became lightheaded and dizzy; one also felt groggy, with numbness of both hands and the tongue, and the other weak, with headache, blurry vision, sweating, warmth and feeling drunk. The two who stayed at the scene developed symptoms there or soon after leaving; one, with blurry vision, warmth, weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness and feeling drunk, was helped out of the room, slumped against the wall and then to the ground, and was given one dose of intranasal naloxone by a colleague, with rapid improvement. Table 1 gives the onset as about 75 minutes after the initial response and about 3 minutes after helping a detained person (the officer given naloxone), about 25 minutes (at headquarters), about 90 minutes (in the ambulance) and about 30–45 minutes after first handling the equipment (the officer who never entered the room); the emergency physicians' impressions were acute dizziness with possible accidental overdose for the officer given naloxone, and dizziness with possible fentanyl exposure for the other three.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 1 (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Before transport all four HHE 2 officers were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing). None was reported to have depressed breathing. In the emergency department all had normal temperatures and normal to raised blood pressure and heart rate; three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth (the officer who never entered the room) a breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; all were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms showed no abnormality. Three had blood tests that ruled out conditions including volume depletion and low blood sugar; the officer given naloxone had no blood test. The urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates. All four were discharged after several hours of observation, with their symptoms improved.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4, continued on p. 5)

key_findings.finding: In evidence from the hotel room the forensic laboratory identified dibutylone (residue), N-ethylpentylone (powder, solid material and residue, 2.87 g), heroin (powder, 0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl (residue; temporarily placed in Schedule I), cocaine and methamphetamine (residue, and liquid in a syringe) and fentanyl (powder and residue, 0.14 g); the Results summarize these as opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones.
key_findings.locator: Results › HHE 2, 3rd paragraph, last sentence (PDF p. 5); Table 2 (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: The authors judge that the officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature. They write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit that continuum, and that the improvement of the officer given naloxone suggests opioids were a substantial component of the mixed exposure; low-level exposure to opioids combined with other drugs, particularly stimulants, might be consistent with the variety of effects, and adulterants or contaminants in illicit drugs might also lead to a variety of effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Health Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms in the Results or Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Perceived risk can be associated with anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure; the relationships between perceived risk, the exposures and the officers' clinical status were not assessed, and the authors suggest adapting validated tools in future investigations.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Health Effects, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing and absorption through the skin, alone or together, are named as the possible routes, and all were possible in both incidents. The authors state that brief skin contact with fentanyl powder, or powder of an analogue, is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (citing three sources, among them the ACMT and AACT statement); that contaminated gloves or hands followed by touching the face can lead to mucous membrane exposure; and that alcohol-based hand sanitizer, as the HHE 1 officer used, may increase absorption of fentanyl powder and should be avoided.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Risk Characterization — Hazard and Exposure, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The negative urine screens do not rule out exposure: routine opiate screens detect opioids derived from the poppy or metabolized to morphine, such as heroin, and will not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl; synthetic cathinones are not readily detected by most amphetamine screens; the amphetamine and cocaine screens of the HHE 2 officers were negative at cut-offs of 500 ng/mL and 150 ng/mL, results below a cut-off being reported as negative; and the timing of testing relative to exposure adds uncertainty.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Issues Related to Risk Characterization — Hazard and Exposure, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: retrospective evaluations, with interviews weeks to months after the incidents; no standardized clinical or toxicological guideline for the clinicians; only the acute emergency department records were reviewed, so other medical conditions could not be assessed afterwards; and toxicological data were not always available because testing followed clinical need. The authors also call these evaluations, to their knowledge, the only organized review of such exposures among emergency responders to date.
key_findings.locator: Investigation Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusions and prevention: multiple drugs, including opioids such as fentanyl and stimulants such as cocaine or methamphetamine, were present at each incident; the effects were not consistent with severe, life-threatening opioid toxicity but needed medical attention and kept the officers from their duties; the authors write that the potential for risk is clear from these investigations, that assuming both that the effects merely reflect perceived risk and that no protective measures are needed endangers responders and the people they help, and that prevention (controls, protective equipment, training on actual against perceived risk) should start now; they call for surveillance, laboratory simulations, guidelines for medical evaluation and timely prospective toxicological testing, noting that serum fentanyl peaks within minutes of an intravenous or transmucosal dose and that urine detection windows vary.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF pp. 1–2); Prevention for First Responders, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 8–9); Next Steps, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 9–10); Conclusion (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: No funding source for the work or the article; the authors declare no conflicts of interest; ethics review was judged unnecessary (a public health activity), with written consent for the release of medical records; all seven authors are at NIOSH.
key_findings.locator: Title block and footnotes (PDF p. 1); Funding (PDF p. 10)

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the officers reported non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness (PDF p. 5), but nausea appears nowhere among the symptoms given for any of the five officers in the Results or Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the symptom list that the authors place on the continuum of opioid effects is not the officers' own; the Results and Table 1 are the ones to cite for the symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: One HHE 2 officer, the one who handled items at headquarters and never entered the room, had an emergency department breathing rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute, whose lower end is below the normal resting range the article gives for the HHE 1 officer (12 to 15 a minute), yet the article states that none of the four was reported to have depressed breathing and does not discuss the low reading or when it was taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: What the reading of 9 reflected cannot be told from the article; the statement that no officer had depressed breathing rests on what was reported, not on this value.

reporting_issues.issue: The years (2017 and 2018) and the states of the two incidents are given only for the pair, never for each incident; only the titles of references 10 and 11 hint at which report belongs to which incident.
reporting_issues.consequence: The date of each incident is unknown; this matters little for the findings but makes it harder to match the incidents with news reports or other evaluations.

design_detail: Online pilot survey (cross-sectional, on SurveyMonkey), open from 1 February to 31 March 2019, of police, fire and emergency medical services (EMS) workers. It was spread by a flyer with a link and QR code, sent with a cover letter and an email to 15 associations of first responders in New York and nationally (3 acknowledged and said they would share it), by flyers at the authors' universities and informally by first responders linked to those institutions. 247 responses; the analysis was limited to the 187 from responders serving New York State (92 in law enforcement; 95 in fire, EMS or both). Fifteen statements on fentanyl risk, each answered on six levels from strongly disagree to strongly agree and reported only as agree or disagree by occupation (Table 2), plus questions on knowledge (gloves, naloxone, protective equipment, information sources) and on demographics. Descriptive; no test results are reported. Published as a Brief Report; read in its typeset online-first version.
can_establish: What these 187 self-selected New York State responders answered in February and March 2019: the share who agreed that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, overall and in law enforcement against fire and EMS; their answers to 14 other statements on fentanyl risk and protection; their choice of gloves; and the information sources they named.
cannot_establish: How common these beliefs were among New York State or US first responders (no sampling frame, 3 of 15 associations sharing the survey, an unknown base and no response rate); how strongly they were held (the six answer levels are reported only as agree or disagree); where any belief came from (sources were not linked to answers); what responders do at scenes; or whether the beliefs are right (the survey measured beliefs, not exposure or harm).

sample.recruitment: Convenience sample: a flyer with the survey link and QR code, with a posted cover letter and an email, went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally, asking chiefs to tell their members; 3 acknowledged and said they would share it; flyers were also posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it informally (PDF p. 2, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph). Agencies did not have to say whether they had shared it (PDF p. 2, Methods, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: First responders. After collection the analysis was limited to the 187 responses from responders serving New York State, because no other state had more than 9 responses (PDF p. 2, Results, 1st paragraph); the other 60 responses (editors' subtraction, 247 − 187) are not described.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (PDF p. 2), by discipline and size of population served: law enforcement 92 (41 serving under 25,000 people, 25 serving 26,000 to 75,000, 9 serving 76,000 to 125,000, 3 serving 126,000 to 250,000 and 14 serving over 250,000); EMS 55 (27 serving over 250,000); fire and EMS dual role 25; fire 15. A majority of every discipline had more than 15 years of experience (no figures), and 53.5% had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work (editors' calculation: 100 of 187) (PDF p. 2, Results, 4th paragraph). Age, sex and rank are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one online survey). Every statement in Table 2 has answers from all 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents and all 92 in law enforcement; whether answers were required is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected respondents reached through the few associations that chose to share the survey, flyers and personal networks; the authors say the study base cannot be known (PDF p. 4, Limitations, 2nd paragraph), so there is no response rate. People more interested in fentanyl safety, or close to the authors' institutions, may be over-represented; EMS respondents came mostly from large agencies (27 of 55 serving over 250,000 people).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study: the groups compared are occupations (law enforcement against fire, EMS or both), as reported by the respondents; 53.5% reported having encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work (self-report, not verified).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (a survey of beliefs and knowledge).

comparison.controls: None outside the sample; Table 2 sets law enforcement (n = 92) beside fire, EMS or dual-role responders (n = 95), without tests.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Training received on fentanyl, years of experience by group, age, sex and rank are not reported; the statement that answers did not vary across demographics comes without figures (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: A questionnaire the authors wrote from a literature review, which experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement are said to have validated for accuracy (no validity or reliability data): 15 statements on fentanyl risk answered on six levels (strongly disagree, disagree, slightly disagree, slightly agree, agree, strongly agree; no middle or do-not-know option), with further questions on knowledge (which gloves are proper, the answers including nitrile, latex and unsure; whether naloxone can treat fentanyl exposure; access to proper protective equipment; information sources, ticking all that apply) and on demographics (PDF p. 2, Methods, 1st paragraph; PDF pp. 2–3, Results). The statement on contact reads "Briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly" (Table 2, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation data. Answers are judged against expert beliefs that are not listed statement by statement; for the contact statement the Discussion treats agreement as contrary to research (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement with each statement, reported only as agree or disagree; the paper does not say how the six levels were grouped or how many respondents chose each, so slight and strong agreement cannot be told apart.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable as reported: no test results are printed, although the authors say some limited statistical tests were performed (PDF p. 2, Methods, 4th paragraph) and that answers did not vary across demographics (PDF p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only, with no intervals. Contact statement: agree 63 of 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents (66.3%) and 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%); 79.7% of all responses in the Discussion (editors' check: 149 of 187; editors' Wilson 95% interval 73.3% to 84.8%; the difference between the groups is 27.2 percentage points, editors' Newcombe interval about 16.0 to 37.7). Breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous: agree 86 of 95 (90.5%) and 92 of 92 (100%) (editors: 178 of 187, 95.2%). Hand sanitizer is safe after handling fentanyl: agree 37 of 95 (38.9%) and 24 of 92 (26.1%), 32.6% in all (editors: 61 of 187). Gloves: nitrile 61.5%, unsure 29.4%, latex 9.1% (editors: 115, 55 and 17 of 187). Naloxone can treat fentanyl exposure: 92% aware. Protective equipment: 76.1% of law enforcement believed they lacked access to proper equipment (editors: 70 of 92), and 55.8% of fire, EMS or dual-role responders believed they had it (editors: 53 of 95). Information sources (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0%, news media 13.9% (editors: 146, 143, 126, 86, 43 and 26 of 187).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the John Jay College of Criminal Justice Institutional Review Board granted an exemption (HRPP file 2018-1578), and an informed-consent statement opened the survey (PDF pp. 2, 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The 15 statements are reported only as agree or disagree; of the knowledge questions only gloves, naloxone, protective equipment and information sources are reported, and the others are not described; the limited statistical tests mentioned are not reported; the 60 responses from outside New York State are set aside without description; and the percentages for gloves, naloxone, equipment and sources carry no denominators (they fit 187, 92 and 95; editors' check).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 187 self-selected New York State responders in February and March 2019, 79.7% agreed, at levels not reported, that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: 93.5% in law enforcement and 66.3% in fire, EMS or both. Most also agreed that breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous (all 92 in law enforcement); 32.6% agreed that hand sanitizer is safe after handling fentanyl; 61.5% chose nitrile gloves as proper (29.4% unsure, 9.1% latex); and most named seminars or courses and department training as information sources, 13.9% the news media.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, with lower agreement on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure (PDF pp. 1, 4): accurate in direction, but the headline does not convey that about 4 in 5 agreed with the contact statement, against the experts' view as the authors present it. The Results claim some generalizability because New York State is diverse (PDF p. 2), which a self-selected sample with an unknown base cannot give. The Discussion suggests that miscommunication and misinformation may have led to the 79.7%, and the Conclusions a possible effect of overreliance on media reports (PDF p. 4), although only 13.9% named news media and 23.0% social media or internet pages, against 78.1% seminars or courses and 76.5% department training (PDF p. 3), and no answer was linked to its source. The Discussion also cites the ACMT and AACT position statement for the view that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods (PDF p. 4), which that statement does not say (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement, cited (reference 9) with a NIOSH video on preventing occupational exposure (reference 8, published March 2019) for guidance that rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact with fentanyl as very low (PDF pp. 1, 5), and again for harm from touching being chronic (PDF p. 4), which it does not say.
This survey, February and March 2019; published online in 2019 (PDF pp. 1–2).
Winograd et al.: before overdose-response trainings in Missouri in 2019, about 1 in 5 of 140 responders answered False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl.

Attaway et al. cite this survey (as Persaud and Jennings, 2019) for nearly 80% of New York first responders believing that even briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (Attaway et al., p. 2). The 79.7% figure is right, but the survey reported agreement at levels it does not give, with law enforcement at 93.5% and fire and EMS at 66.3%, and its statement says briefly, not even briefly.
del Pozo et al.: before trainings in Indiana in 2020 and 2021, 103 of 129 officers (79.8%) agreed that responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it.

replication.where_it_stands: About 4 in 5 agreeing with a statement on danger from touching fentanyl recurs in the baselines of two training surveys by another team, whose authors partly overlap (Missouri and Indiana), each with a different statement, and none of the three is a random sample. This is the only survey on file whose statement concerns death rather than overdose, and the only one that reports information sources as numbers, though not linked to the belief. No probability sample of first responders is on file.

funding.funder: No funding source for the work or the article, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies (PDF p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at John Jay College of Criminal Justice (CUNY), New York, and Persaud also at SUNY Downstate Medical Center (PDF p. 4). Jennings conceived the study, Persaud designed the instrument, and Paul Landsbergis gave feedback on its design (PDF p. 4). The authors share no author with the other surveys on file. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a random sample drawn from complete rosters of New York State (or US) police, fire and EMS staff, with a known response rate and follow-up of non-respondents, using tested statements reported at every answer level, asking separately about touching, breathing in and contact with the eyes or mouth, and linking each answer to the training and information sources the person received and to what they do at scenes.
