risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any estimate of how common these beliefs were among New York State first responders: a self-selected sample with no frame and no response rate, measured with untested statements collapsed into agree or disagree. The survey may be cited for what its 187 respondents answered (for example, 149 of 187 agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, more often in law enforcement than in fire and EMS) and for the information sources they named; not for the share of first responders in general who hold the belief, for where the belief came from, for what responders do, or for whether touching fentanyl is dangerous.

key_findings.finding: Methods: the authors wrote the questionnaire from a literature review, and experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement are said to have validated it for accuracy; it had fifteen 6-point statements on risk perception (strongly disagree, disagree, slightly disagree, slightly agree, agree, strongly agree) and further questions on knowledge and demographics, with consent on its opening page. It ran on SurveyMonkey from 1 February to 31 March 2019, confidentially; a flyer with the link and a QR code went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally (15 letters and 15 emails, asking chiefs to tell their members), flyers were posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it; one response per device; the aim was mainly descriptive, with some limited statistical tests.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 247 responses were received; 187 came from first responders serving New York State and no other state had more than 9, so the analysis was limited to New York. Of the 15 associations, 3 acknowledged and said they would share the survey; it took about 5 minutes to complete. Because agencies did not have to say whether they shared it, the authors cannot ascertain the overall study base.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 2); Limitations, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Respondents by discipline (Table 1): law enforcement 92, EMS 55, fire and EMS dual role 25, fire 15 (187); the authors describe the law enforcement respondents as fairly evenly distributed across sizes of population served, although Table 1 shows 41, 25, 9, 3 and 14 from the smallest to the largest, while 27 of the 55 EMS respondents served populations over 250,000. A majority of all disciplines had more than 15 years of experience, and 53.5% of EMS, law enforcement and fire/EMS personnel (fire-only responders are not named) had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work. Note: 53.5% fits 100 of 187, and also 92 of 172 without the 15 fire-only responders (editors' calculation), so the denominator is uncertain; no figures are given for experience.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: 53.5% fits 100 of 187 (editors' calculation); no figures are given for experience.

key_findings.finding: Briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: agree 63 of 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents (66.3%), disagree 32 (33.7%); agree 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%), disagree 6 (6.5%). The Discussion gives 79.7% of responses agreeing.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, row on briefly touching fentanyl (PDF p. 3); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 149 of 187 = 79.7%, Wilson 95% interval 73.3% to 84.8%; the six levels are reported only as agree or disagree.

key_findings.finding: Other statements (agree, fire, EMS or dual role of 95; law enforcement of 92): breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous to my health 86 (90.5%), 92 (100%); you should not touch your face after handling fentanyl 90 (94.7%), 91 (98.9%); it is safe to disturb fentanyl without protective equipment if you use caution 12 (12.6%), 5 (5.4%); fentanyl in pill form is safe to handle 40 (42.1%), 13 (14.1%); the only type of fentanyl that is a health risk to me is the powder form 17 (17.9%), 2 (2.2%); fentanyl has the same strength as morphine 16 (16.8%), 18 (19.6%); I can see the signs and symptoms of a fentanyl overdose 77 (81.1%), 71 (77.2%); it is safe to use hand sanitizer after handling fentanyl 37 (38.9%), 24 (26.1%); gloves should be changed regularly 83 (87.4%), 80 (87%); it is safe to eat, drink or smoke when handling fentanyl 3 (3.2%), 2 (2.2%); I would not be concerned about needing emergency treatment for exposure 26 (27.4%), 6 (6.5%); I would not be worried about having difficulty breathing 26 (27.4%), 2 (2.2%); I am concerned about covering my nose and mouth 68 (71.6%), 90 (97.8%); I am not worried about protecting my eyes and face 20 (21.1%), 3 (3.3%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: Protective measures: 92% knew that naloxone could be used to treat exposure to fentanyl; asked which gloves are proper for handling suspected fentanyl, 61.5% chose nitrile, 29.4% were unsure and 9.1% chose latex; 76.1% of law enforcement respondents believed they did not have access to proper protective equipment, while 55.8% of fire, EMS or dual-role respondents believed they did; fire and EMS respondents were nearly split on whether fentanyl in pill form is safe to handle (42.1% agreeing), while 85.9% of law enforcement disagreed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Protective Measures, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 2, continued on p. 3); 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Information sources on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0% and news media 13.9%; the authors conclude that a sizable majority relies on official sources, specialized courses and departmental training being the most common.
key_findings.locator: Results › Information Sources, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
key_findings.note: Sources were asked about fentanyl exposure and safety in general and are not linked to any answer, including the contact statement.

key_findings.finding: Discussion: respondents understood the need to protect the eyes, face, mouth and nose, and answers did not vary across demographics (no figures). The authors name four main issues: 32.6% agreeing that hand sanitizer is safe after fentanyl exposure (which, they write, would spread fentanyl and may increase absorption); 38.5% unable to identify nitrile as the proper glove; 79.7% agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, which they suggest miscommunication and misinformation may have caused, writing that research has shown brief contact is not deadly and harms no one who washes the skin thoroughly with soap and water, and that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods (citing reference 9); and law enforcement believing they lack proper protective equipment, while fire and EMS respondents believe they have it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3, continued on p. 4) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: Reference 9 is the ACMT and AACT position statement, which does not contain the chronic-harm statement (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Introduction: initial concerns over hazards to responders may have been heightened by early warnings from law enforcement sources (reference 7, a Drug Enforcement Administration nationwide alert on fentanyl published in March 2015); since then, guidance from authoritative sources rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact with fentanyl as very low (reference 8, a NIOSH video on preventing occupational exposure, published in March 2019, and reference 9, the 2017 ACMT and AACT statement); and sensational media reports of often non-specific symptoms after casual exposure have become commonplace (reference 10, a New York Times editorial of April 2019).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 4th paragraph (PDF p. 1, right column); references 7 to 10 (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: The paper does not mention the Drug Enforcement Administration's roll-call training video that other papers on file date to 2016 (Attaway et al., 2021) or to 6 June 2017 (Herman et al., 2020).

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-reported data, which some respondents may have given differently from their behaviour in the field; an online survey, chosen for confidentiality, that limited follow-up; the overall study base cannot be ascertained; and future studies should use in-person systematic sampling, wider samples in other states and nationally, follow-up interviews or focus groups, and paired items to check reliability. Conclusions: respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, but not on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure; larger samples are needed to validate the findings; the knowledge gaps reflect a need for better training through authoritative sources, and a possible effect of overreliance on media reports of adverse effects from casual exposure.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Funding: none, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies; no conflict-of-interest statement; exempted by the John Jay College of Criminal Justice Institutional Review Board (HRPP file 2018-1578).
key_findings.locator: Funding; Institution and Ethics approval and informed consent

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites the 2017 ACMT and AACT position statement (reference 9) for the view that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue, more likely in people who touch it regularly or for long periods (PDF p. 4). The statement on file contains no such passage; its opening position and its section on long-term effects say that, in the absence of prolonged lack of oxygen, no persistent effects are expected after exposure (Moss et al., 2017, PDF pp. 1, 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The chronic-harm statement has no support in the source cited for it, and the paper should not be cited for it.

reporting_issues.issue: The 15 statements were answered on six levels but are reported only as agree or disagree, without saying how the levels were grouped or how many respondents chose each.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 79.7% agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly cannot be split into strong and slight agreement, so how firmly the belief was held is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 3 of the 15 associations acknowledged and distributed the survey (PDF p. 1); the Results say 3 acknowledged and said they would distribute it (PDF p. 2), and the Methods that agencies did not have to say whether they had (PDF p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the 3 associations actually shared the survey, and with how many people, is unknown; no response rate can be computed.

reporting_issues.issue: The knowledge questions are neither listed nor counted; only gloves, naloxone, protective equipment and information sources are reported, so whether other questions went unreported cannot be told; the Results call the Table 2 statements questions on general knowledge, while the Methods call them risk-perception items; the limited statistical tests mentioned in the Methods are not reported; the statement that answers did not vary across demographics comes without figures; and the percentages for gloves, naloxone, equipment and sources have no stated denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be ruled out; the counts behind the percentages can be recovered (they fit 187, 92 and 95; editors' check).

design_detail: CDC surveillance report (MMWR) from the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS), in which participating jurisdictions abstract unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths from death certificates, postmortem toxicology reports and medical examiner or coroner reports. Two analyses: (1) the quarterly percentage of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, July 2019 to December 2021, in 30 jurisdictions (29 states and the District of Columbia) with complete data, 106,293 deaths; (2) characteristics of 2021 deaths with (2,437) and without (52,331) such evidence in 35 jurisdictions (34 states and DC), 54,768 deaths. Evidence of counterfeit pill use was found by text searches of each death's free-text narrative (substrings such as 'counterf' or 'M-30', brand names when the drug was absent on toxicology) and the SUDORS counterfeit-pill checkbox; flagged narratives were coded by two coauthors, with discrepancies resolved by consensus (p. 949, Methods and footnotes §, ¶ and **). Descriptive percentages only, with no statistical tests. Filed as registry (surveillance records) and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist.
can_establish: How often SUDORS records of overdose deaths in these jurisdictions documented evidence of counterfeit pill use in 2019–2021, how that share changed by census region, and how decedents with such evidence differed descriptively from other decedents in 2021.
cannot_establish: The risk of death from using a counterfeit pill, what share of counterfeit pills contain fentanyl, or that the pills caused the deaths: pill contents were not tested in most cases (the number tested is not reported), pills found at a scene may not have been used, and the authors expect documentation to underestimate counterfeit pill use, unevenly between and within jurisdictions.

sample.recruitment: Records of unintentional and undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths reported to SUDORS. Arkansas, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Washington (and, for 2021, Louisiana) reported deaths only from counties accounting for at least 75% of the state's 2017 overdose deaths, per SUDORS funding requirements; the other jurisdictions reported all deaths (p. 949, footnotes § and ¶).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Jurisdictions with complete data, including medical examiner or coroner reports for at least 75% of deaths, for the whole period (July 2019 to December 2021 for trends; 2021 for characteristics); analysis restricted to decedents with an available medical examiner or coroner report (p. 949, footnotes § and ¶). Adulterant analyses limited to IMF-involved deaths with toxicology reports: 2,258 with and 37,352 without evidence of counterfeit pill use (Table 1 footnote †††, p. 952). n_total is the trend sample; the 2021 sample overlaps it.
sample.demographics: 2021, deaths with versus without evidence: median age 32 (IQR 25–42) vs 43 (33–54); male 71.9% vs 70.6%; Hispanic or Latino 18.7% vs 9.4%; White non-Hispanic 61.2% vs 66.2%; Black or African American non-Hispanic 13.9% vs 21.2%; American Indian or Alaska Native non-Hispanic 3.2% vs 1.6% (Table 1, p. 951).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Missing values were excluded from percentages (Table 1 footnote †, p. 952); jurisdictions without complete data were excluded.
sample.selection_effects: Only 30 (trends) and 35 (2021) jurisdictions met the completeness criteria, covering part of each census region (trends: 8 of 9 Northeast, 5 of 12 Midwest, 9 of 17 South and 8 of 13 West jurisdictions; footnote §§, p. 950); the authors say results may not generalize beyond them (p. 955, Limitations). Ascertainment of counterfeit pills depends on scene investigation and the completeness of examiner reports, which the authors expect to vary within and between jurisdictions (p. 955).

exposure.measurement: Evidence of counterfeit pill use, any of five criteria: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit (by witnesses, law enforcement, medical examiners or coroners); pills testing positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; pills appearing as oxycodone with no oxycodone on postmortem toxicology, or appearing as alprazolam with no alprazolam detected; unmarked pills; or a witness report of pill use when none of the drugs detected is available in legitimate pill form (p. 950, Methods continued). Counterfeit type coded as oxycodone, alprazolam, both, or unspecified (p. 949, footnote **). How many deaths met each criterion, and how many involved laboratory-tested pills, is not reported; agreement between the two coders is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Only non-ingestion routes are presented, because the counterfeit-pill definition depends largely on evidence of pill use and SUDORS guidance records ingestion when pills are found (Table 1 footnote ****, p. 952).
exposure.polysubstance: A drug counts as involved if listed as a cause of death on the death certificate or examiner report; categories are not mutually exclusive (Table 1 footnote ¶). 'IMFs only' means IMFs were the only drugs listed as cause of death; ethanol was not counted as a drug, so some of these deaths also involved alcohol (footnote ††). Fentanyl was classed as illicitly manufactured from toxicology, scene and witness evidence, and the 8% of fentanyl deaths with insufficient evidence were classed as illicit; all fentanyl analogues except alfentanil, remifentanil and sufentanil counted as IMFs (footnote **, p. 952).

comparison.controls: 2021 overdose deaths without documented evidence of counterfeit pill use (n = 52,331) in the same 35 jurisdictions; for trends, comparison across census regions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: whether decedents knew a pill was counterfeit, pill contents in most cases, opioid tolerance and frequency of use, and how documentation practice differed between jurisdictions or changed over 2019–2021.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Deaths without documented evidence may include undocumented counterfeit pill use, since documentation is likely incomplete (p. 955, Limitations), so the comparison group is contaminated to an unknown degree.

outcomes.instruments: Quarterly percentage of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use, overall and by census region (Figure, p. 950); characteristics of deaths with and without evidence (Table 1, p. 951) and by counterfeit pill type (Table 2, p. 953).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the narrative-based definition against pill testing is reported; the authors expect underestimation, and note that pills found or reported at the scene may be counted even if the decedent did not use them (p. 955, Limitations).
outcomes.operationalization: Pills marked M-30 found at the scene or reportedly used were defined as counterfeit oxycodone if no oxycodone was detected on postmortem toxicology (Table 2 footnote §§§, p. 954). A potential bystander is a person aged 11 or older nearby who may have had an opportunity to respond (Table 1 footnote ††††, p. 952).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests or confidence intervals are reported; all comparisons are descriptive percentages.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to record coding; coders saw toxicology results, which are part of the definition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Trend (30 jurisdictions): 2.0% of overdose deaths in July–September 2019 to 4.7% in October–December 2021; western jurisdictions 4.7% to 14.7%; all other regions below 4% throughout (p. 950, Results, 1st paragraph; Figure). 2021 (35 jurisdictions; Table 1, p. 951; with vs without evidence): 2,437 of 54,768 deaths (4.4%) had evidence; any IMF involved 93.0% vs 72.2%; IMFs only 41.4% vs 19.5%; illicit benzodiazepines 5.3% vs 1.4%; any stimulant 39.6% vs 55.5%; heroin 5.2% vs 12.6%; aged under 35 57.1% vs 28.1%; West 55.8% vs 16.3%; history of prescription drug misuse 27.0% vs 9.4%; smoking 39.5% vs 17.3%; snorting 33.5% vs 14.2%; injection 11.5% vs 19.6%; naloxone administered 26.7% vs 20.8%; potential bystander present 64.5% vs 44.4%; fatal drug use witnessed 25.2% vs 7.8%. No tests, intervals or adjusted comparisons; the number of deaths with evidence in each quarter of the trend analysis is not printed.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Surveillance report; the activity was reviewed by CDC and conducted consistent with applicable federal law and CDC policy (p. 950).
analysis.selective_reporting: Ingestion and 'no route' evidence are deliberately not presented because they depend on the definition (Table 1 footnote ****). Quarterly numerators and regional denominators are not printed. The 55.1% smoking figure for western jurisdictions (p. 953) appears in no table.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Documented evidence of counterfeit pill use rose from 2.0% to 4.7% of overdose deaths in 30 jurisdictions between mid-2019 and late 2021, after peaking at about 5.1% in April–June 2021 (Figure), and from 4.7% to 14.7% in eight western jurisdictions. In 2021, deaths with such evidence more often involved only IMFs (41.4% vs 19.5%), and the decedents were younger, more often Hispanic and more often had a history of prescription drug misuse than other decedents.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion infers that, because counterfeit pills often contain IMFs and only IMFs were involved, the pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death (p. 954, Discussion, 3rd paragraph); how many deaths had pills tested is not reported, and the definition includes pills found at the scene and unmarked pills. The Discussion reads the western rise as IMFs infiltrating western drug markets (p. 954, 2nd paragraph), which is an inference from a share of death records. The abstract and summary present prevention messaging and drug product testing as measures that could help prevent overdose deaths (p. 949; p. 956), framed as possibilities and not tested here. The report states its limitations (p. 955).

timeline.event: Green and Gilbert (2016), cited for white-powder IMFs having been less prevalent in western states because of difficulty mixing them with the black tar heroin common there (p. 954, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; ref. 3). Not read.

Palamar et al. (2022): in HIDTA seizure records, fentanyl-containing pill seizures rose from 13.8% to 29.2% of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures between early 2018 and late 2021; cited by this report (ref. 2) for the proliferation of counterfeit pills (card sc_palamar_2022).
Daniulaityte et al. (2022), cited for the possibility that smoking reflects ways of using counterfeit pills (p. 955, Discussion, 5th paragraph; ref. 9). Not read.
This report (MMWR, 1 September 2023).

replication.where_it_stands: Seizure records (Palamar et al., 2022) and these death records agree that counterfeit pills became a larger part of the US fentanyl problem in 2019–2021, with western states most affected in the death records. The share of deaths involving counterfeit pills is likely underestimated (authors), documentation practice may have changed over the period, and no study read for this card measures the share of street pills that contain fentanyl.

funding.funder: No funding statement is printed. All authors are at CDC's Division of Overdose Prevention, National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, one also at the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (p. 956). Data come from jurisdictions participating in CDC's Overdose Data to Action (OD2A) programme and providing data to SUDORS (p. 956, Acknowledgments); reporting follows SUDORS funding requirements (p. 949, footnote §).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors completed and submitted the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors form for disclosure of potential conflicts of interest; no potential conflicts of interest were disclosed (p. 956).
funding.affiliations_note: CDC runs and funds the surveillance system, wrote the report and issues the prevention recommendations it makes (messaging, fentanyl test strips, drug-checking services). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Systematic laboratory testing of pills found at overdose scenes and of pills bought on the street, with standard scene-investigation and narrative protocols across jurisdictions and over time, so that the share of overdose deaths involving counterfeit pills, and the share of pills containing fentanyl, can be estimated without depending on how complete each narrative is.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample

domains.domain: 8. Appropriate statistical analysis

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large census of death records with an explicit, double-coded definition. The main threat is ascertainment: evidence of counterfeit pill use depends on scene investigation and narrative completeness, is expected to be underestimated unevenly by place and possibly over time, and rarely rests on tested pills. Citable for: the share of overdose deaths with documented evidence of counterfeit pill use in these jurisdictions (2.0% in mid-2019, 4.7% in late 2021, 14.7% in the West), and the characteristics of these deaths in 2021, as descriptive minimums. Not citable for: the true share of deaths caused by counterfeit pills, the risk per pill used, the fentanyl content of pills, or causal statements about routes, bystanders or naloxone.

key_findings.finding: In 30 jurisdictions (106,293 overdose deaths, July 2019 to December 2021), the quarterly share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use rose from 2.0% (July–September 2019) to 4.7% (October–December 2021); in western jurisdictions it rose from 4.7% to 14.7%; in all other regions it stayed below 4%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 949); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 950); Figure (p. 950)

key_findings.finding: Read from the Figure (approximate): the total share was about 2.3% (October–December 2019), 3.8% (April–June 2020), 4.2% (October–December 2020), 5.1% (April–June 2021) and 4.9% (July–September 2021) before 4.7% at the end of 2021; the western share was about 7.3% in late 2019 and early 2020, 10.0% in mid-2020, 13.2% in late 2020 and early 2021, 14.0% in April–June 2021 and 13.4% in July–September 2021. The Discussion says the overall share stayed below 6% (p. 954).
key_findings.locator: Figure (quarterly lines by census region)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of the Figure; approximate. Quarterly numerators are not printed.

key_findings.finding: In 2021, 2,437 of 54,768 overdose deaths in 35 jurisdictions (4.4%) had evidence of counterfeit pill use; 55.8% of these deaths occurred in western jurisdictions, against 16.3% of deaths without such evidence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 950); Table 1 (p. 951)

key_findings.finding: Drugs involved, 2021, deaths with vs without evidence of counterfeit pill use: any IMF 93.0% vs 72.2%; IMFs as the only drugs listed as cause of death 41.4% vs 19.5%; illicit benzodiazepines 5.3% vs 1.4%; any stimulant 39.6% vs 55.5%; heroin 5.2% vs 12.6%. Among IMF-involved deaths with toxicology, xylazine was detected in 2.1% vs 7.9%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 949); Table 1 and footnotes (pp. 951–952); Results, 2nd paragraph (continued, p. 952)

key_findings.finding: Decedents with evidence of counterfeit pill use were younger (median age 32 vs 43; aged under 35, 57.1% vs 28.1%; aged 15–24, 22.4% vs 5.7%), more often Hispanic or Latino (18.7% vs 9.4%), and more often had a history of prescription drug misuse (27.0% vs 9.4%) or a previous overdose (14.7% vs 10.9%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 949) and Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 950) for the under-35 shares; Table 1 (p. 951) for the rest
key_findings.note: Table 1 prints age bands, not the under-35 total; 57.1% and 28.1% are printed in the Abstract and Results and recompute from Table 1 (1,391 of 2,437; 14,698 of 52,325 with age known; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Routes and circumstances, with vs without evidence: smoking 39.5% vs 17.3% (55.1% among western deaths with evidence), snorting 33.5% vs 14.2%, injection 11.5% vs 19.6%; naloxone administered 26.7% vs 20.8%; overdosed at home 67.3% vs 62.6%; potential bystander present 64.5% vs 44.4%; fatal drug use witnessed 25.2% vs 7.8%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnotes **** and §§§§ (pp. 951–952); Results, 2nd paragraph (continued, pp. 952–953)
key_findings.note: Bystander presence and witnessed use may be overrepresented among deaths with evidence because the definition partly depends on these circumstances (Table 1 footnote §§§§); ingestion is not presented for the same reason.

key_findings.finding: By counterfeit pill type (2021): oxycodone only 1,346 deaths (55.2%), alprazolam only 415, both 95 (3.9%), unspecified 581. Pills marked M-30 were documented in 889 (66.0%) oxycodone-only and 31 (32.6%) combined deaths. IMFs were the only drugs involved in 49.9% (oxycodone only), 19.0% (alprazolam only) and 32.6% (both); illicit benzodiazepines in 1.5%, 17.1% and 18.9%. Western jurisdictions accounted for 66.4% of oxycodone-only and 43.2% of combined deaths; southern jurisdictions for 42.2% of alprazolam-only deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 953, continued on p. 954); Table 2 (p. 953) and footnote §§§ (p. 954)

key_findings.finding: Decedents were youngest when both counterfeit oxycodone and alprazolam were documented: median age 26 (IQR 22–35); 40.0% were aged 15–24 and 73.7% under 35.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 953); Results, 3rd paragraph (continued, p. 954)

key_findings.finding: Definition of evidence of counterfeit pill use: pills at the scene identified as counterfeit; pills testing positive for drugs other than what they appeared to contain; oxycodone- or alprazolam-looking pills with that drug absent on postmortem toxicology; unmarked pills; or witness-reported pill use with no detected drug available in legitimate pill form. Deaths were flagged by checkbox or substring searches and narratives coded by two coauthors.
key_findings.locator: Methods, footnote ** (p. 949); Methods, continued (p. 950, left column, top)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: results may not generalize beyond the included jurisdictions; documentation of counterfeit pill use relied on the completeness of examiner and coroner reports, is likely underestimated, and underestimation likely varies within and between jurisdictions; the definition included pills found or reported at the scene, so some deaths may be counted even if the decedent did not use the pills.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, single paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results report the trend as a change from the first to the last quarter (2.0% to 4.7%, more than doubled), but the total share peaked at about 5.1% in April–June 2021 and was lower in the last two quarters (Figure); no trend test or intervals are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the first-to-last-quarter change and describe the second half of 2021 as a plateau or slight fall, not as continued growth.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use in each quarter, and the regional denominators, are not printed, so the trend percentages cannot be checked or combined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Regional and quarterly percentages can be cited only as printed or read from the Figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion infers that the counterfeit pills used likely contained the drugs that caused death (p. 954), but the report does not say how many deaths involved pills that were laboratory-tested, and its definition includes unmarked pills and pills found at the scene that may not have been used (p. 955).
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Evidence of counterfeit pill use' should not be written as 'death caused by a counterfeit pill'.

reporting_issues.issue: Potential bystander presence and witnessed fatal drug use are compared between deaths with and without evidence of counterfeit pill use, although the report notes that the definition partly depends on these circumstances (Table 1 footnote §§§§).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bystander and witnessing differences (64.5% vs 44.4%; 25.2% vs 7.8%) are partly built into the definition and should not be cited as findings about people who use counterfeit pills.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says nearly one half of deaths with evidence of counterfeit alprazolam only were in southern jurisdictions; Table 2 gives 175 of 415 (42.2%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 42.2%.

reporting_issues.issue: The smoking percentage for western jurisdictions (55.1%, p. 953; '>50%' in the Discussion, p. 955) is given only in the text, with no table or denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the figure cannot be checked.

design_detail: Secondary trend analysis of aggregate quarterly law-enforcement seizure records, January 2018 to December 2021 (16 quarters), from the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA) programme: 33 HIDTAs located in 50 states and the District of Columbia, whose participating federal, state, local and tribal agencies report seizures quarterly to the HIDTA Performance Management Process; data obtained through a collaboration between HIDTA and the National Drug Early Warning System (NDEWS) (PDF p. 3, 2.1 Procedure). Any fentanyl or fentanyl analogue detected in a seized product was coded as a fentanyl seizure (PDF p. 3, Introduction, 3rd paragraph). Units are seizure events and seized amounts, not people or individual pills. Outcomes: quarterly numbers of fentanyl-containing powder seizures and pill seizures, the share of pill seizures among pill-plus-powder seizures, the total weight of powder seized and the total number of pills seized. Generalized additive models with automatically selected knots were plotted with 95% confidence bands, and polynomial terms up to cubic were then tested and the best-fitting model reported for each series (PDF p. 3, 2.2 Statistical analyses). Filed as registry (law-enforcement records) and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for seizure data.
can_establish: How many fentanyl-containing powder and pill seizures HIDTA-participating agencies recorded per quarter in 2018–2021, and that pills became a larger share of these seizures (13.8% of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures in January–March 2018, 29.2% in October–December 2021).
cannot_establish: What share of counterfeit or street pills contain fentanyl (the denominator is fentanyl-containing seizures, not pills), how much fentanyl pills held, what seized pills were made to look like, where in the country the changes happened (no regional breakdown), whether the changes reflect the drug supply rather than policing, testing and reporting, or any link with overdose in these data.

sample.recruitment: Records, not people: drug seizures made by agencies participating in HIDTAs, collected quarterly from all HIDTAs by the HIDTA Performance Management Process and examined through the HIDTA–NDEWS collaboration (PDF p. 3, 2.1 Procedure). n_total is null because the total number of seizures over the 16 quarters is not reported; only first- and last-quarter values are printed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Seizures in which fentanyl or a fentanyl analogue was detected, January 2018 to December 2021. Only pill and powder forms are analysed: the printed pill share equals pill seizures divided by pill-plus-powder seizures (68/492 = 13.8% and 635/2174 = 29.2%, editors' calculation), so any other forms are outside the denominator. How fentanyl was detected (laboratory or field testing), whether all seized products were tested, and how many agencies reported in each quarter are not described.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Completeness of reporting across HIDTAs and quarters is not described.
sample.selection_effects: Seizures reflect where and how intensively law enforcement acts, and what it tests and reports, as well as what is on the market; HIDTAs are designated trafficking areas, not the whole country. The authors note that seizures are meant to reduce supply and that studies of seizures as indicators of availability show mixed results (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 4th paragraph). The Introduction cites a DEA enforcement surge in August–September 2021 that seized 1.8 million pills (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 2nd paragraph); whether such operations are in the HIDTA data and contribute to the 2021 peaks is not discussed.

exposure.measurement: Detection of any fentanyl or fentanyl analogue in a seized product, as coded by HIDTAs; analogues cannot be separated from fentanyl (PDF p. 3, Introduction, 3rd paragraph; PDF p. 6, 4.1 Limitations). Testing method and purity are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (seizure records). No information on the amount of fentanyl per pill or the purity of powders (PDF pp. 5–6, 4.1 Limitations).
exposure.polysubstance: Not available: the data cannot show whether a seized product held fentanyl alone or fentanyl combined with another drug such as cocaine (PDF pp. 5–6, 4.1 Limitations).

comparison.controls: No comparison group: trends over 16 quarters, and pill seizures set against powder seizures.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to records. Not measured or not available: what seized drugs were sold as and what pills were pressed to resemble (for example oxycodone or alprazolam), fentanyl content, co-occurring drugs, markings, the number of agencies reporting each quarter, testing practice, and changes in enforcement priorities (PDF pp. 5–6, 4.1 Limitations).

outcomes.instruments: Quarterly counts of fentanyl-containing powder seizures and pill seizures; the proportion of pill seizures among pill-plus-powder seizures; total weight (kg) of fentanyl powder seized; total number of fentanyl-containing pills seized (PDF p. 3, 3. Results; Fig. 1, PDF p. 10; Fig. 2, PDF p. 11).
outcomes.validity_norms: Seizure counts are a supply indicator of uncertain validity. The authors cite studies linking fentanyl seizures with synthetic-opioid deaths (PDF p. 3, Introduction, 3rd paragraph) and a review finding mixed links between seizures and availability (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Fentanyl seizure' means any fentanyl or analogue detected in the product; each seizure event counts once regardless of its size; the pill share is pill seizures over pill-plus-powder seizures.

analysis.effect_sizes: Endpoint comparisons, 2018 Q1 to 2021 Q4 (PDF p. 3, 3. Results): powder seizures 424 to 1539, a 263.0% increase (linear trend, β = 0.94, SE 0.09, p < 0.001); pill seizures 68 to 635, an 833.8% increase (quadratic, β = 0.96, SE 0.24, p < 0.01); pill share 13.8% to 29.2%, a 111.6% relative increase (β = 0.92, SE 0.10, p < 0.001); weight of powder seized 298.2 kg to 2416.0 kg, a 710.2% increase (quadratic, β = 1.12, SE 0.38, p = 0.01); pills seized 42,202 to 2,089,186, a 4850.4% increase (described as linear, β = 0.90, SE 0.12, p < 0.001). All five percentages recompute from the endpoint values (editors' calculation). The β coefficients are not defined (scale or standardization not stated), and no confidence intervals for the changes, yearly totals or period totals are given. Editors' calculation: about 621 pills per pill seizure in 2018 Q1 and about 3290 in 2021 Q4, so the rise in pills seized partly reflects larger seizures.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned. Secondary analysis judged not to involve human subjects and exempt from review by the NYU Langone Medical Center institutional review board (PDF p. 3, 2.2 Statistical analyses).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only first- and last-quarter values are printed; the quarterly series appears only in Figs 1–2. The model-selection criterion, the error distribution and any handling of autocorrelation or seasonality across the 16 quarters are not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; each trend rests on 16 quarterly points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In HIDTA records, fentanyl-containing seizures rose in 2018–2021 and pills made up a growing share of them: 29.2% of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures in the last quarter of 2021, against 13.8% at the start of 2018; pills seized per quarter rose from about 42 thousand to about 2.1 million. All four count series were below their 2021 peaks in the final quarter, and the final pill share was the series high (Figs 1–2).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions say that, because over a quarter of fentanyl seizures are now pills, people who obtain counterfeit pills, such as pills disguised as oxycodone or alprazolam, are at risk of unintentional fentanyl exposure (PDF p. 2, Abstract › Conclusions; PDF p. 6, 4.2 Conclusions). The data hold no information on what seized pills were made to resemble (PDF p. 6, 4.1 Limitations), so that link rests on cited literature rather than on these data, although it is plausible. The Discussion treats seizures as indicating availability while acknowledging mixed evidence (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 4th paragraph). The 'over a quarter' figure is a share of fentanyl seizures, not of pills, and the paper does not claim otherwise; it cannot say what share of pills contain fentanyl.

timeline.event: US DEA, NFLIS-Drug 2020 Annual Report, cited: significant increases in fentanyl seizures between 2018 and 2020, without separating pills from powders (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 3rd paragraph); the authors say their results corroborate NFLIS data (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 3rd paragraph). Not read.

Palamar et al. (2021a), cited: fentanyl seizures kept increasing through the COVID-19 pandemic while cannabis and methamphetamine seizures dipped and rebounded (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 3rd paragraph). Not read.
This study (published in final form 1 May 2022).

O'Donnell et al. (2023), CDC: in 30 US jurisdictions the share of overdose deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use rose from 2.0% (July–September 2019) to 4.7% (October–December 2021), and from 4.7% to 14.7% in western jurisdictions; the report cites this study (card sc_odonnell_2023).

replication.where_it_stands: Two different US indicators, seizures (this study) and deaths with evidence of counterfeit pill use (O'Donnell et al., 2023), both show counterfeit pills taking a growing part in fentanyl exposure in 2019–2021. Neither gives the share of street pills that contain fentanyl; the pill-content figures the authors quote come from DEA laboratory statements, not from these data.

what_would_settle_it: Laboratory testing of a random or complete sample of seized and street-purchased pills, recording what each pill was made to resemble and its fentanyl content, reported with the numbers of pills and seizures tested, stable reporting coverage over time and a regional breakdown, and linked by place and quarter to overdose data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A national series of law-enforcement records, transparently reported at its endpoints. As a description of recorded seizures the risk of bias is moderate: coverage, testing and coding practice are not described, the series is reported only at its first and last quarters, and the trend models are underspecified. As an indicator of the drug supply the risk is high, because seizures depend on policing priorities and reporting, as the authors acknowledge. Citable for: HIDTA-recorded fentanyl seizures rose in 2018–2021; pills rose from 13.8% to 29.2% of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures; pills seized per quarter rose to about 2.1 million by late 2021. Not citable for: the share of pills containing fentanyl, fentanyl amounts, what pills were made to look like, regional patterns, or links with deaths.

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl-containing powder seizures rose from 424 in January–March 2018 to 1539 in October–December 2021, a 263.0% increase (linear trend, β = 0.94, SE 0.09, p < 0.001).

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl-containing pill seizures rose from 68 to 635 over the same quarters, an 833.8% increase (quadratic trend, β = 0.96, SE 0.24, p < 0.01).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, single paragraph; Fig. 1, left panel (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Pill seizures as a share of pill-plus-powder fentanyl seizures rose from 13.8% (2018 Q1) to 29.2% (2021 Q4), a 111.6% relative increase (β = 0.92, SE 0.10, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, single paragraph; Fig. 1, right panel (PDF p. 10)
key_findings.note: The denominator is pill plus powder seizures (68/492 = 13.8%; 635/2174 = 29.2%, editors' calculation). This is a share of fentanyl seizures, not the share of pills that contain fentanyl.

key_findings.finding: The weight of fentanyl powder seized rose from 298.2 kg in 2018 Q1 to 2416.0 kg in 2021 Q4, a 710.2% increase (quadratic trend, β = 1.12, SE 0.38, p = 0.01).

key_findings.finding: The number of fentanyl-containing pills seized rose from 42,202 in 2018 Q1 to 2,089,186 in 2021 Q4, a 4850.4% increase (described as linear, β = 0.90, SE 0.12, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, single paragraph; Fig. 2, right panel (PDF p. 11)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: about 621 pills per pill seizure in 2018 Q1 and about 3290 in 2021 Q4.

key_findings.finding: Read from the figures (approximate): powder seizures peaked at about 2050 in 2021 Q3 and pill seizures at about 675 in 2021 Q3; the weight of powder seized peaked at about 2920 kg in 2021 Q2; pills seized peaked at about 2.73 million in 2021 Q2, with a dip from about 1.76 million (2020 Q3) to about 0.88 million (2020 Q4). The quarterly pill share fluctuated (about 0.215 in 2019 Q3, about 0.173 in 2019 Q4), and its final value (0.292) lies above the fitted curve (about 0.27).

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that using seizures as an indicator of availability may seem counterintuitive, since seizures aim to reduce supply, and that studies of seizures and availability show mixed results; they argue that rising seizures alongside rising synthetic-opioid deaths point to greater overall availability.

reporting_issues.issue: The β coefficients are not defined: their scale or standardization is not stated, and for the quadratic models it is not said which term β refers to.
reporting_issues.consequence: The β values cannot be interpreted as amounts of change; cite the endpoint counts instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The fitted curve for the number of pills seized (Fig. 2, right) is visibly curved, although the text calls this trend linear. The Methods say the plotted curves are generalized additive model splines and that the reported β values come from separately chosen polynomial models, without stating the selection criterion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model whose β is reported is not the one drawn; the shape of the trend cannot be checked against the printed statistics.

reporting_issues.issue: Fitted curves and 95% bands extend below zero at the start of the series: the fitted number of pills seized is about −0.1 million in 2018 Q1 with the band reaching about −0.58 million, the powder-weight band reaches about −40 kg, and the pill-seizure band dips slightly below zero (read from Figs 1–2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Impossible values suggest normal-error models fitted to counts; with no stated handling of autocorrelation, the p values are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: All percentage changes compare two single quarters. The final quarter was below the 2021 peak in all four count series, and the final pill share is the highest point of its series (Figs 1–2); no yearly or period totals are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the changes as first-to-last-quarter figures, not as average growth; percentages such as 4850.4% are sensitive to the quarters chosen.

reporting_issues.issue: The estimate that about 2 mg of fentanyl can be lethal and the statement that 42% of pills tested by the DEA contained at least that amount are cited from DEA web pages and testimony, not drawn from this study's data, which contain no amounts per pill.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be cited from this paper; a claim using them must cite and check the DEA source.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the pill share the proportion of pills to total seizures, but the printed values equal pill seizures over pill-plus-powder seizures (editors' calculation); other forms of fentanyl seizure, if any, are outside the denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; describe the share as pills among pill and powder seizures.
